Chapter 1 · Part I · The idea

Start here

You said you know nothing about the field, so this guide starts from nothing. You will meet every idea before the code that uses it. Nothing is skipped, and nothing assumes you remember a word from school.

By the end you will be able to explain, in your own words, how a computer scored a resume against a job, how it explained that score, and how it read a PDF to do it. You will also be able to read every line of the project's code.

How the guide is organised

  1. Part I explains the problem and the plan, with no code.
  2. Part II teaches the tools: just the Python, machine learning, text and explanation ideas this project uses.
  3. Part III walks through every source file, in the order the pipeline runs.
  4. Part IV shows the results, how to run it all, and a quiz.

How to read a code chapter

Each code chapter shows the real file in small pieces. The code is on the left. A plain-language explanation of exactly those lines is on the right. Line numbers match the real file, so you can open the file next to this page.

51def normalize_skill(skill: str) -> str:
52 s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", skill.strip().lower())
Lines 51–52

This is what a code chapter looks like. The grey tag above says which lines this explanation covers. Read the code first, then the words beside it. On a phone the explanation moves under the code.

The four kinds of note

Coloured boxes appear throughout. Each has one job:

Analogy

A picture from everyday life that makes an idea feel familiar.

Remember

The two or three things from a chapter worth keeping.

Careful

A trap, an honest limit, or a real bug we hit while building this.

Try it

A command to run yourself. Reading teaches you less than doing.

A suggested route

  • First time through: read chapters 1 to 5 properly, then go through the code chapters in order. Do not try to memorise anything.
  • Short on time: read 1 and 2, the first half of 4, then chapter 16.
  • Before presenting: chapters 4, 10 and 16 cover what examiners ask about.

Two habits will help more than anything else. When a line confuses you, run it in a terminal and look at the result. And when a word is new, check the glossary in the last chapter.

Words you will meet straight away

Do not try to learn these now. Just notice them. Each is explained properly later.

Dataset
A table of examples. Here, 600 resume-and-job pairs.
Feature
A number that measures one useful thing, such as “share of required skills present”.
Label
The correct answer for an example. Here, good match (1) or poor match (0).
Model
A program that learned from examples how to turn features into an answer.
SHAP
A method that explains how much each feature pushed a prediction up or down.
Chapter 2 · Part I · The idea

The problem and the plan

The problem

A company opens a job and receives 400 resumes. Nobody has time to read them all, so software ranks them. Many such tools give each candidate a score and nothing else.

That is a problem for two reasons. A recruiter cannot tell why a candidate scored 40, so cannot decide whether to trust it. A candidate cannot tell what to fix. And when a decision affects someone's career, “the computer said so” is not good enough. A program whose reasoning cannot be seen is called a black box.

Your presentation states the goal in one line:

Prediction + Explanation = Trust

So the project must do two things for every candidate: predict how well they match the job, and explain the prediction in terms a person understands.

The plan

The plan has the shape of a factory line. Raw material goes in at the left (a resume and a job), and each station changes it a little until a score and a reason come out at the right.

Resume + Jobtext→ Read & cleanparse, normalize skills→ 7 numbersfeatures→ Logistic Regressionthe model→ Probability0 to 100%→ SHAPthe reasons→ Words + chartfor a human

Two phases use this line:

  • Learning phase (done once). We build thousands of examples, convert them to numbers, and let the model learn from them. Files: author_dataset.py, feature_engineering.py, train_model.py.
  • Using phase (done every time you use the app). A new job and new resumes go through the same line, and the already-trained model gives scores. Files: resume_parser.py, matcher.py, app.py.

The explanation step (explain_shap.py, report_candidate.py) works in both phases.

The folder map

Here is everything in the project folder and what each part is for.

Resume Matching/ ├─ app.py the web app you click on ├─ requirements.txt the list of libraries to install ├─ README.md the short instructions ├─ Resume_Matcher_Guide.html this page ├─ src/ the program, one job per file │ ├─ skills.py skill nicknames and whole-word search │ ├─ author_dataset.py makes the 600 practice resumes and the answers │ ├─ feature_engineering.py turns words into 7 numbers │ ├─ train_model.py teaches the model │ ├─ explain_shap.py draws the explanation charts │ ├─ report_candidate.py writes the slide 7 report │ ├─ resume_parser.py reads PDF, Word and text resumes │ ├─ matcher.py ranks applicants for a job │ └─ generate_dataset.py optional: AI-written resumes ├─ data/ │ ├─ jobs.json the 10 job postings │ ├─ resumes.json the 600 resumes with answers │ ├─ dataset.csv the table of numbers the model learns from │ └─ v1_backup/ the first, weaker version of the data ├─ outputs/ │ ├─ model.pkl the trained model (tiny) │ ├─ tfidf.pkl the text-similarity tool, saved │ ├─ metrics.json the exam marks │ ├─ X_test.csv, y_test.csv the hidden exam questions and answers │ ├─ shap_*.png the explanation charts │ └─ shap_explanations.json every test candidate's reasons └─ sample_resumes/ 8 example resumes to upload

What is real and what is simulated

This matters, and it is the first thing a careful examiner will ask.

  • Real: the code, the machine learning method, the SHAP explanations, the parser, and the app. These all genuinely work.
  • Simulated: the 600 resumes and, more importantly, the answers. No company hired anyone. A small program standing in for a recruiter decided who was a good match.

So the accuracy figure tells you how well the model learned the simulated recruiter's tastes. It does not tell you how well it would do in a real company. Your own slide 8 says this: synthetic training data may not fully represent real hiring scenarios. We repeat it here because it is true and because honesty is part of the project.

Remember
  • The goal is prediction and explanation, not prediction alone.
  • The pipeline turns text into numbers, numbers into a probability, and a probability into reasons.
  • The data and labels are simulated. The method is real.
Chapter 3 · Part II · The tools you need

Python, just what this project uses

The whole project is written in Python, a language designed to read almost like English. You do not need to learn all of Python. This chapter teaches only the parts the project uses. Each idea has a small example, and under every example you can see exactly what Python prints. These outputs were produced by really running the code, on this project's own files.

How to read the grey boxes

Open a terminal, type python, press Enter, and you get a prompt that looks like >>>. That is Python's console: you type one line and it answers at once. In the boxes below, a line that starts with >>> is what you type. A line starting with ... continues the line above. The blue lines are what Python answers. Do not type the >>> or the blue lines. If you select and copy a box, only the code is copied. Type exit() to leave the console.

1. What running a program means

A Python file is a list of instructions in a text file. When you run python src/train_model.py, Python reads the file from the top and does each instruction in order. It stops at the end or at an error. That is all a program is: instructions, followed one at a time. Here is the smallest real one. Save the text below in a file called hello.py, then run it:

hello.pySave this as a file
# This line is a comment. Python skips it.
name = "Priya"
print("Hello,", name)
print(2 + 3)
Run itIn a terminal, in the same folder
$ python hello.py
Hello, Priya
5

The comment line printed nothing, print showed text on screen, and the lines ran from top to bottom.

A terminal is the window where you type commands. A comment starts with #. Python ignores everything after it on that line, so comments are notes for people.

2. Values and variables

A variable is a name stuck on a value, like a label on a jar. The sign = does not mean “equals” here. It means “put this value in that jar”.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> years = 5               # a whole number
>>> score = 0.91            # a decimal number
>>> name = "Priya"          # text, always inside quotes
>>> is_good = True          # True or False (a "boolean")
>>> nothing = None          # a special value meaning "no value"
>>> print(years, score, name, is_good, nothing)
5 0.91 Priya True None
>>> years + 2               # a variable works like the value it holds
7
>>> type(score)             # ask Python what kind of value this is
<class 'float'>
>>> type(name)
<class 'str'>

Maths works as you would expect, with a few extras that appear in the project:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> 7 / 2     # normal division
3.5
>>> 7 // 2    # whole-number division (drops the remainder)
3
>>> 7 % 2     # the remainder
1
>>> 2 ** 3    # two to the power three
8

3. Text and f-strings

An f-string is text with an f in front. Anything in curly brackets is replaced by its value, and you can format it.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> x = 0.9066
>>> f"Accuracy is {x:.3f}"        # 3 decimals
'Accuracy is 0.907'
>>> f"That is {x*100:.0f}%"       # 0 decimals
'That is 91%'
>>> f"R{7:04d}"                   # pad to 4 digits
'R0007'
>>> f"{'Ava':<10}|"               # left-align, width 10
'Ava       |'

Useful text tools, all shown running below: .strip() (trim spaces), .lower() (small letters), .split(",") (cut into a list), ", ".join(list) (glue a list into text), .replace(a, b) (swap text).

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> "  Hello, SQL  ".strip()                  # trim spaces at both ends
'Hello, SQL'
>>> "SQL".lower()                             # small letters
'sql'
>>> "python,sql,excel".split(",")             # cut into a list
['python', 'sql', 'excel']
>>> ", ".join(["python", "sql", "excel"])     # glue a list into text
'python, sql, excel'
>>> "I use k8s".replace("k8s", "kubernetes")  # swap text
'I use kubernetes'

4. Collections: four ways to hold many things

NameLooks likeKey factsWhere we use it
list["python", "sql"]Ordered. Can repeat. You can add and remove.Skill lists, rows, results.
tuple("Data Scientist", 3)Ordered. Fixed once made.(title, description) pairs.
set{"python", "sql"}No order. No duplicates. Fast to compare.Counting skill overlap.
dict{"title": "Data Scientist", "years": 3}Pairs of key and value. Look up by key.Every job, every resume, every result.
Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> pair = ("Data Scientist", 3)
>>> pair[0]
'Data Scientist'
>>> pair[0] = "Analyst"       # a tuple cannot be changed after it is made
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

The error above is deliberate. It shows what a Python complaint looks like: a Traceback header, then the kind of error (TypeError) and a plain-English reason. The last line is the one that matters.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> skills = ["python", "sql", "excel"]
>>> skills[0]          # counting starts at 0
'python'
>>> skills[-1]         # the last one
'excel'
>>> skills[:2]         # the first two: a "slice"
['python', 'sql']
>>> len(skills)
3
>>> skills.append("r") # adds to the end
>>> skills
['python', 'sql', 'excel', 'r']

>>> job = {"title": "Data Scientist", "min_experience": 3}
>>> job["title"]
'Data Scientist'
>>> job.get("salary", "unknown")  # a default if the key is missing
'unknown'
>>> job["min_experience"] = 4     # change a value
>>> job
{'title': 'Data Scientist', 'min_experience': 4}

Sets have maths-style operations, which is why the project uses them for skills:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> a = {"python", "sql", "pandas"}
>>> b = {"sql", "excel"}
>>> a & b     # in both  (intersection)
{'sql'}
>>> a | b     # in either (union)
{'python', 'pandas', 'sql', 'excel'}
>>> a - b     # in a but not b
{'python', 'pandas'}
>>> len(a & b) / len(a)   # the share of a that b has
0.3333333333333333
>>> {"sql", "sql", "python"}   # duplicates vanish
{'python', 'sql'}

A set has no order, so Python may print the same items in a different order on your machine. The members are what matter.

5. Making decisions

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> years = 2
>>> if years >= 3:
...     verdict = "senior"
... elif years >= 1:
...     verdict = "junior"
... else:
...     verdict = "entry"
... 
>>> verdict
'junior'

Here years is 2, so Python skipped the first test (2 is not at least 3), passed the second (elif), and stopped. Change the first line to years = 5 and the answer becomes 'senior'.

Indentation (the spaces at the start of a line) is how Python knows which lines belong inside the if. It is not decoration. Comparisons are == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, >=. Combine them with and, or and not.

The project often uses a short form called a conditional expression, which reads like a sentence:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> prob = 0.72
>>> label = "good" if prob >= 0.5 else "poor"
>>> label
'good'
>>> prob = 0.31
>>> "good" if prob >= 0.5 else "poor"
'poor'

One more habit. In a condition, an empty list, empty text, 0 and None all count as False. So title or "Open role" means “use title, but if it is empty, use ‘Open role’”. You will see this pattern often. Here it is running:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> bool([]), bool(""), bool(0), bool(None)       # all "empty", so all False
(False, False, False, False)
>>> bool(["python"]), bool("Rahul"), bool(7)      # all "something", so all True
(True, True, True)
>>> title = ""
>>> title or "Open role"       # empty, so the fallback is used
'Open role'
>>> title = "Data Analyst"
>>> title or "Open role"       # not empty, so title is kept
'Data Analyst'

6. Loops

A loop repeats instructions.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> for skill in ["python", "sql"]:
...     print(skill)
... 
python
sql

>>> for i in range(3):           # i is 0, then 1, then 2
...     print(i)
... 
0
1
2

>>> for i, skill in enumerate(["python", "sql"]):   # gives a counter too
...     print(i, skill)
... 
0 python
1 sql

>>> for name, years in zip(["Ava", "Liam"], [3, 5]):  # walk two lists together
...     print(name, years)
... 
Ava 3
Liam 5

break leaves a loop early. continue skips to the next round. Here they both run:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> for n in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
...     if n == 2:
...         continue        # skip the rest of this round
...     if n == 4:
...         break           # leave the loop completely
...     print(n)
... 
1
3

The 2 was skipped (continue), and the loop ended at 4 (break), so 4 and 5 never printed. Handy built-in helpers that appear in the code: sum, min, max, len, sorted, any (true if at least one item is true) and all.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> nums = [3, 9, 5]
>>> sum(nums), min(nums), max(nums), len(nums)
(17, 3, 9, 3)
>>> sorted(nums)
[3, 5, 9]
>>> sorted(nums, reverse=True)
[9, 5, 3]
>>> any([False, True, False])    # is at least one True?
True
>>> all([False, True, True])     # are they all True?
False

7. Comprehensions: loops written as one line

These look strange at first and then become your favourite thing in Python. Read them from left to right as a sentence.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> [s.lower() for s in ["SQL", "Python"]]          # list
['sql', 'python']
>>> {s.lower() for s in ["SQL", "sql", "Python"]}   # set (the duplicate vanishes)
{'python', 'sql'}
>>> jobs = [{"id": "J01", "title": "Data Scientist"}, {"id": "J02", "title": "ML Engineer"}]
>>> {j["id"]: j["title"] for j in jobs}             # dict: id -> title
{'J01': 'Data Scientist', 'J02': 'ML Engineer'}
>>> [x for x in [1, 5, 8] if x > 3]                 # with a filter
[5, 8]

The last form means “for each x, keep it if it is above 3”. The project uses all four shapes.

8. Functions

A function is a named recipe. You write it once and use it many times.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> def share(have, need, strict=False):
...     """Fraction of 'need' that 'have' covers."""      # a docstring
...     if not need:
...         return 0.0
...     return len(have & need) / len(need)
... 
>>> share({"sql"}, {"sql", "python"})
0.5
>>> share({"sql"}, set())                                    # nothing was needed
0.0
>>> share(have={"sql", "python"}, need={"sql", "python", "excel"})   # arguments by name
0.6666666666666666
  • def starts it. have, need are parameters, the inputs.
  • strict=False is a default. You may leave it out when calling.
  • return sends back the answer and ends the function. A function can return several things, as return a, b.
  • The text in triple quotes is a docstring, a note for humans.
  • You will see hints such as def f(x: str) -> int. They say what goes in and out. Python does not enforce them. They help readers.

A lambda is a tiny function with no name, written on one line: lambda kv: kv[1] means “given kv, return its second item”. It is mostly used to say how to sort:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> pairs = [("sql", 3), ("python", 9), ("excel", 5)]
>>> sorted(pairs, key=lambda kv: kv[1])                  # smallest second item first
[('sql', 3), ('excel', 5), ('python', 9)]
>>> sorted(pairs, key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)    # biggest second item first
[('python', 9), ('excel', 5), ('sql', 3)]

The path prints as WindowsPath on Windows and PosixPath on Mac or Linux. Both mean the same thing. The with blocks print nothing: they just did their work quietly. The last line then read the file back, so you can see that json.dump really wrote it.

JSON is a plain-text format for lists and dictionaries, which almost every language understands. A CSV is a table saved as text, one row per line, columns separated by commas. Spreadsheets open both.

The pandas library works with tables. A DataFrame is a table inside Python:

10. When things go wrong

An error (also called an exception) stops the program with a message. You can plan for them:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> data = "café".encode("latin-1")     # bytes that are NOT valid UTF-8
>>> data.decode("utf-8")                # unprotected: the program would stop here
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 3: unexpected end of data

>>> try:
...     text = data.decode("utf-8")
... except UnicodeDecodeError:        # only this kind of error
...     text = data.decode("latin-1") # try something else instead
... 
>>> text
'café'

>>> raise ValueError("Unsupported file type")   # you can stop on purpose, with a message
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: Unsupported file type

The project uses this to show a friendly message when a file is missing or a resume cannot be read, instead of a confusing crash.

11. Importing, and the “main” guard

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import re                       # borrow a whole toolbox; use as re.something
>>> re.findall(r"\d{4}", "2019 and 2021")
['2019', '2021']
>>> import pandas as pd             # borrow it under a short nickname
>>> pd.__version__
'3.0.2'
>>> from pathlib import Path        # borrow just one tool
>>> Path("data").exists()
True

>>> import sys
>>> sys.path.insert(0, "src")       # tell Python to look in our src folder too
>>> from skills import mentions     # borrow from one of OUR files (skills.py)
>>> mentions("I know JavaScript", "java")
False
>>> mentions("I know java.", "java")
True

The last two answers come from our own mentions function. It says False for “JavaScript” because we want the whole word java, not the same letters inside another word. The regex section of this part explains how.

Almost every script in the project ends with these two lines:

greet.pySave this as a file
print("1. file loaded, __name__ is:", __name__)

def main():
    print("2. main() is running")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Run itIn a terminal, in the same folder
$ python greet.py
1. file loaded, __name__ is: __main__
2. main() is running
$ python -c "import greet"
1. file loaded, __name__ is: greet

When you run a file directly, Python sets a special name __name__ to "__main__", so main() runs. When another file merely imports it, the name is different and nothing runs. That lets files share their functions safely.

12. Classes, just enough

A class is a blueprint for bundling data with the functions that use it. The project has exactly one: Artifacts in matcher.py.

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> class Counter:
...     def __init__(self):        # runs automatically when you create one
...         self.n = 0             # "self" means: this particular object
...     def add(self):
...         self.n += 1            # += means "add to"
... 
>>> c = Counter()                  # build an object from the blueprint
>>> c.add(); c.add()
>>> c.n
2
>>> d = Counter()                  # a second object has its own memory
>>> d.n
0

Chapter 4 · Part II · The tools you need

Machine learning from zero

What machine learning is

Normally you write rules for a computer: if the candidate has all the required skills, score high. The trouble is that real decisions have too many rules, and the rules interact. Machine learning flips the process. You give the computer many examples with the right answers, and it works out the rules itself.

Analogy

You teach a child to recognise ripe mangoes. You do not hand over a rulebook. You hold up mangoes, say “ripe” or “not ripe”, and after fifty examples the child has learned that yellow and slightly soft means ripe. Then you test with a mango the child has never seen. That is the whole idea: learn from examples, then test on new ones.

Our task is a classification problem: put each candidate into one of two groups, good match or poor match.

Examples, features and labels

An example is one row of data, here one resume compared with one job. Each example has two kinds of information:

  • Features: the inputs. Numbers that describe the example. We use seven.
  • Label: the right answer. 1 means good match, 0 means poor match.

Here are two real rows from dataset.csv:

RowRequired skillsPreferredExperienceEducationTechProjectsSimilarityLabel
R0000, Product Manager job0.601.001.251.000.331.000.271 good
R0004, ML Engineer job0.000.000.670.410.000.330.180 poor

R0004 is a Fine Arts graduate whose resume lists testing and cloud tools, applying for a machine learning engineer role. The numbers capture why that is a poor match: no required skills, no tools, a partly wrong degree. A model sees only the seven numbers, never the story.

Practice set and exam set

If you test a student on the questions they practised, you only measure memory. So we hide a quarter of the data. The model learns from the practice rows and is marked on the exam rows it has never seen. This is the train/test split.

450 practice rows (75%)
150 exam (25%)

Training means finding good weights. Now let us see what a weight is.

Logistic Regression in three steps

Our model is called Logistic Regression. Despite the name, it classifies. It is deliberately simple, which is exactly why it is used when you want to explain a result: every number inside it can be read.

Step 1: a weighted sum

Give each feature a weight, meaning how much it matters. Multiply each feature by its weight, add them all up, and add one starting number (the intercept). The total is a raw score z. For our trained model:

score = -5.80 +4.48 x required_skill_match +1.24 x preferred_skill_match +0.68 x experience_match +0.81 x education_match +1.12 x technology_match +2.06 x project_relevance +0.60 x semantic_similarity

The biggest weight is on required skills (4.48), then projects (2.06). The model learned that required skills matter most. We never told it that. The simulated recruiter weighted required skills highest (chapter 7), and the model rediscovered it from examples.

Step 2: squash the score into a probability

The raw score z can be any number, from very negative to very positive. A probability must sit between 0 and 1. The sigmoid function squeezes any number into that range:

probability = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) where e is about 2.718

You can compute this yourself. These few lines are the whole function:

Try the sigmoidType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import math
>>> def sigmoid(z):
...     return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
... 
>>> sigmoid(0)         # a coin flip
0.5
>>> sigmoid(2)
0.8807970779778823
>>> sigmoid(-2)
0.11920292202211755
>>> sigmoid(4)
0.9820137900379085
>>> sigmoid(-5.8)      # our model's intercept alone: before any feature adds anything
0.003018416324708424

Those are the same numbers as the table below.

raw score zprobabilityreading
−42%almost certainly poor
−212%probably poor
050%a coin flip
+288%probably good
+498%almost certainly good

Step 3: apply a cut-off

If the probability is 0.5 or more, the model says good match. Otherwise poor match. The probability itself is your “compatibility score” (slide 5).

A worked example

Take Arjun Johnson (R0001) from chapter 8, whose seven features we saw. Multiply each by its weight:

Featurevalueweightvalue × weight
required_skill_match0.4004.48+1.79
preferred_skill_match0.0001.24+0.00
experience_match1.3330.68+0.90
education_match1.0000.81+0.81
technology_match0.2501.12+0.28
project_relevance0.6672.06+1.38
semantic_similarity0.1090.60+0.06

Add the products, add the intercept (-5.80), and the raw score is -0.57. The sigmoid turns that into 36%, below 0.5, so the model says “poor match”. The recruiter's real label for this row was good match, so here the model got it wrong. A model that is right 91% of the time is wrong 9% of the time. Rows like this one are what that 9% looks like.

Play with the real model

Below is the actual trained model, with its real weights. Choose a candidate or drag the sliders and watch the probability move. The bars on the right show why: how far each feature pushed the score up (green) or down (red) compared with an average applicant. That is SHAP, in action.

Choose a candidate, or drag the sliders

What the trained model says

0%

Why (SHAP contributions, bigger bar = bigger push)

Things to try
  • Pick Poor fit, then drag Required skills to 1. How far does the probability jump? That one slider moves it more than any other.
  • Pick Great skills, no experience. The model still says good, because experience has a small weight. A real recruiter might disagree. This is a real limitation of the model, and it is why the app has an optional “hard requirement” filter.
  • Set every slider to 0, then raise only Text similarity to its maximum. It barely helps. That feature has the smallest weight.

How we measure the model

After training, the model answers the 150 exam questions. Every answer is one of four kinds. The table of those four counts is called the confusion matrix. These are the real numbers from our model:

Predicted poor
Predicted good
Actually poor
87correct (true negatives)
7false alarms (false positives)
Actually good
7missed (false negatives)
49correct (true positives)

From those four numbers come the standard scores. Each answers a different question:

ScoreQuestion it answersOur arithmeticResult
AccuracyOf all answers, how many were right?(49 + 87) ÷ 1500.907
PrecisionWhen the model says “good”, how often is it right?49 ÷ (49 + 7)0.875
RecallOf the truly good candidates, how many did it find?49 ÷ (49 + 7)0.875
F1One number balancing precision and recall2 × P × R ÷ (P + R)0.875
ROC-AUCIf you pick one good and one poor candidate at random, how often does the model score the good one higher?measured over all cut-offs0.956

Why so many scores? Because accuracy alone can mislead. If only 5% of candidates were good, a model that always said “poor” would be 95% accurate and completely useless. Precision and recall expose that.

In hiring the two kinds of mistake cost different things. A false alarm wastes a recruiter's interview. A miss unfairly rejects a good person. Which matters more depends on the company, and you should say so when you present.

Cross-validation

One exam of 150 questions can be lucky or unlucky. So we repeat the practice-and-exam cycle five times, each time hiding a different fifth of the data, and average the results. Our accuracy this way is 0.932, with the five marks differing by about 0.013. A small spread means the model is stable. Our first, smaller dataset (100 rows) gave folds from 0.75 to 1.00, which was a sign the data was too small to trust.

Overfitting

A model overfits when it memorises the practice questions instead of learning the pattern. It then scores very high in practice and poorly on the exam. We guard against it by (1) always scoring on held-out data, (2) using a simple model with only 8 numbers to learn, which has little room to memorise, and (3) cross-validating.

What can go wrong, in general

  • Garbage in, garbage out. A model copies whatever pattern its labels contain. If the labels are biased, the model will be too. Resume screening is a sensitive area, which is why your slides list fairness and bias analysis as future work. Our model never sees names, ages or genders. But related details can still act as stand-ins, so real systems must be audited.
  • Simulated labels. Ours come from a small program, so a high score means “it learned our program”.
  • Explanations are not proof. SHAP shows what the model did. It cannot show that the model was right.
  • A weighted sum is rigid. It cannot say “without three years of experience, reject, whatever else is true”. A different model type could.
Remember
  • Machine learning = learn rules from labelled examples, then test on unseen ones.
  • Logistic Regression = weighted sum → sigmoid → probability → cut-off at 0.5.
  • Always report more than accuracy, and always test on data the model has not seen.
  • Our model's weights are readable, which is why explanation is easy.
Chapter 5 · Part II · The tools you need

Text, patterns and explanations

Three more ideas show up in the code, and they are the ones that look most mysterious: patterns for finding text, a way to measure how similar two texts are, and the explanation method itself. Each gets its own section here, so the code chapters can stay short.

Regular expressions: a language for describing text patterns

You know the “Find” box in a word processor. It finds the exact letters you typed. A regular expression (regex) is a Find box that can describe shapes of text: “four digits in a row”, “a word followed by an @ sign”. The resume parser depends on them to find dates, emails, degrees and headings.

Analogy

Telling a security guard “let in anyone called Rahul” is a plain search. Telling him “let in anyone with a badge that starts with two letters, then four digits” is a regex. You described the shape of a badge, not a particular one.

The building blocks

PatternMeansMatches in …
abcexactly those letters“abc”
.any one character“a”, “7”, “#”
\done digit“7”
\wone letter, digit or underscore“k”, “_”
\sone space, tab or line break“ ”
[a-z]one character from the set“q”
[^a-z]one character not in the set“Q”, “5”
x+one or more of x\d+ in “2024”
x*zero or more of xab* in “a”, “abbb”
x?x is optional (zero or one)colou?r in “color” and “colour”
x{4}, x{1,2}exactly 4 / between 1 and 2\d{4} in “2019”
a|ba or bphd|doctor
( )group, and remember what matched(\d{4})
(?: )group only, do not remember(?:in|of)
^ and $start and end of the text (or line)^Hello
\bthe edge of a word\bmba\b not in “embark”
(?= )lookahead: what comes next must be this, but do not consume itjava(?=\s)
(?<! )negative lookbehind: what came before must not be this(?<![a-z])java
\.a backslash makes a special symbol literala real dot

The Python functions that use them

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import re
>>> re.search(r"\d{4}", "Joined in 2019")                 # finds the first match anywhere
<re.Match object; span=(10, 14), match='2019'>
>>> re.search(r"\d{4}", "Joined in 2019").group()          # the matched text itself
'2019'
>>> re.search(r"\d{4}", "no year here")                    # no match gives None (nothing is printed)
>>> re.fullmatch(r"skills", "Skills", flags=re.I)         # the WHOLE text must match (ignoring capitals)
<re.Match object; span=(0, 6), match='Skills'>
>>> re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "a   b \n c")                     # replace matches
'a b c'
>>> re.findall(r"(\d{4})\s*-\s*(\d{4})", "2019 - 2021")    # all matches, as pairs
[('2019', '2021')]
>>> pattern = re.compile(r"\d{4}")                        # prepare a pattern once, reuse it
>>> pattern.findall("2018, 2020 and 2023")
['2018', '2020', '2023']

The r before the quotes makes a raw string: backslashes are left alone. Always use it for patterns. Common flags: re.I (ignore capitals), re.M (make ^ and $ work on every line), re.DOTALL (let . match line breaks too).

Building one step by step

Goal: find work date ranges such as “2019 - 2021”.

  1. A year is four digits: \d{4}
  2. A range is a year, a dash, a year: \d{4}-\d{4}
  3. People add spaces: \d{4}\s*-\s*\d{4} (\s* means zero or more spaces)
  4. We want the two years separately, so wrap each in a group: (\d{4})\s*-\s*(\d{4})
Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import re
>>> text = "Data Analyst, Acme Corp, 2019 - 2021"
>>> re.findall(r"\d{4}", text)                    # step 1: every four-digit number
['2019', '2021']
>>> re.findall(r"\d{4}-\d{4}", text)              # step 2: finds nothing, our text has spaces around the dash
[]
>>> re.findall(r"\d{4}\s*-\s*\d{4}", text)        # step 3: allow spaces
['2019 - 2021']
>>> re.findall(r"(\d{4})\s*-\s*(\d{4})", text)    # step 4: capture the two years separately
[('2019', '2021')]

Step 2 found nothing because our text has spaces around the dash, which is why step 3 was needed. That is exactly how the parser's date pattern is made, only with more alternatives (month names, “Present”, other kinds of dash). Real patterns look scary because they are many small steps glued together. Read them from left to right, piece by piece.

The most important pattern in the project

The function mentions(text, term) in skills.py builds (?<![a-z0-9])java(?![a-z0-9]). Read it: “the letters java, but the character before must not be a letter or digit, and the character after must not be either”. So it finds “I know java.” and rejects “javascript”. Before this fix, our first version counted a project about JavaScript as relevant to a Java job, because the letters java sit inside javascript. Watch both versions run:

See the differenceType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import re
>>> "java" in "i know javascript"                 # a plain search is fooled
True
>>> re.search(r"(?<![a-z0-9])java(?![a-z0-9])", "i know javascript")   # our pattern is not (prints nothing)
>>> re.search(r"(?<![a-z0-9])java(?![a-z0-9])", "i know java.")
<re.Match object; span=(7, 11), match='java'>

>>> import sys
>>> sys.path.insert(0, "src")
>>> from skills import mentions                    # the project's own helper
>>> mentions("I know JavaScript", "java")
False
>>> mentions("I know Java.", "java")
True
Careful
  • Regexes are fragile. A pattern that works on ten test files can fail on the eleventh. Keep real samples and re-test.
  • Try patterns interactively at regex101.com. It highlights what matches and explains each part.

TF-IDF and cosine similarity: how alike do two texts sound?

The seventh feature, semantic_similarity, needs a number for “does this resume read like this job advert?”. Computers cannot compare meaning directly, but they can compare words. The method has two steps.

Step 1: turn a text into a list of numbers

Make a vocabulary of all the words, then count how often each appears in each text. Suppose the whole world has only four words:

Textpythonsqlpandasexcel
A: “python sql pandas”1110
B: “python sql excel”1101

Scikit-learn can build this table for you. Run it:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
>>> from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

>>> texts = ["python sql pandas", "python sql excel"]
>>> cv = CountVectorizer()
>>> counts = cv.fit_transform(texts)       # count the words in each text
>>> cv.get_feature_names_out()             # the vocabulary (sorted A to Z)
array(['excel', 'pandas', 'python', 'sql'], dtype=object)
>>> counts.toarray()                       # one row per text: the vectors in the table above
array([[0, 1, 1, 1],
       [1, 0, 1, 1]])
>>> cosine_similarity(counts[0], counts[1]).round(2)
array([[0.67]])

Scikit-learn sorts the vocabulary A to Z, so its columns come in a different order from our table, but each text gets the same numbers. Each text is now a list of numbers, a vector. Think of it as an arrow pointing in a direction in a space with one axis per word.

Step 2: measure the angle between the arrows

Cosine similarity measures how much two arrows point the same way. Two texts with the same words point the same way (score 1). Texts with no words in common point at right angles (score 0).

cosine = (A · B) / (|A| x |B|) A · B = 1x1 + 1x1 + 1x0 + 0x1 = 2 (multiply matching positions, add up) |A| = sqrt(1+1+1+0) = sqrt(3) = 1.73 (the arrow's length) |B| = sqrt(1+1+0+1) = sqrt(3) = 1.73 cosine = 2 / (1.73 x 1.73) = 2 / 3 = 0.67

So A and B are 0.67 similar: they share two of their three words. The code above printed the same 0.67, which confirms the hand calculation.

The improvement: TF-IDF

Plain counts treat every word equally, but “the” and “experience” appear in every resume and tell you nothing. TF-IDF adjusts each count:

  • TF (term frequency): how often the word appears in this text.
  • IDF (inverse document frequency): how rare the word is across all the texts. A word in every text gets a very low weight. A word in only a few texts, like “terraform”, gets a high one.

Multiply them and distinctive words dominate. Our code also removes stop words (the, and, of) with stop_words="english". Here it is on three tiny texts where python appears in all of them:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
>>> from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

>>> texts = ["python sql pandas", "python sql excel", "python terraform"]
>>> tv = TfidfVectorizer()
>>> m = tv.fit_transform(texts)
>>> {w: round(float(v), 2) for w, v in zip(tv.get_feature_names_out(), tv.idf_)}   # how rare each word is
{'excel': 1.69, 'pandas': 1.69, 'python': 1.0, 'sql': 1.29, 'terraform': 1.69}
>>> cosine_similarity(m[0], m[1]).round(2)
array([[0.48]])

python is in every text, so it gets the lowest rarity score. terraform, excel and pandas each appear once, so they score higher. Because python is so common, the similarity of the first two texts falls from 0.67 to 0.48: the word they share counts for less.

Why our similarity numbers are low

Real values sit around 0.1 to 0.5, even for good matches, because a resume and a job advert are written very differently and are long. That is normal. Since it is a weak signal, the model gives it the smallest weight (0.60).

Fit once, transform later

The vectorizer first fits: it reads all 610 texts and learns the vocabulary and each word's rarity. Afterwards it only transforms: it converts a new text using what it already learned. In the app we reload the saved tfidf.pkl and transform. If we fitted a new one, the numbers would be on a different scale, and the trained model would misread them. This is the saved one from our project:

Run itType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import joblib
>>> tfidf = joblib.load("outputs/tfidf.pkl")      # the vectorizer saved by feature_engineering.py
>>> len(tfidf.vocabulary_)                        # how many different words it learned
592
>>> tfidf.transform(["python sql pandas"]).shape  # one text in, one row of 592 numbers out
(1, 592)
Honest limit

TF-IDF sees words, not meaning. “Not experienced in Java” looks almost the same as “experienced in Java”. “Car” and “automobile” look unrelated. Modern systems use embeddings, which capture meaning. That is a natural next step for the project.

SHAP in more depth

Chapter 10 introduced the idea. Here is the substance.

Where it comes from

In 1953 Lloyd Shapley asked: when a team earns a prize together, how do you split it fairly? His answer was to take each member in turn and measure how much they add to the team averaged over every possible order in which the team could have assembled. SHAP applies that to a model. The “team” is the set of features, and the “prize” is the prediction.

The easy case: a linear model

Averaging over every order is expensive in general. For a weighted-sum model like ours, the answer collapses to a short formula:

contribution of a feature = weight x (this candidate's value - average value) starting point (the "base value") = intercept + sum of weight x average final score = base value + all seven contributions

The average comes from the background examples, here all 600 rows. You can run the calculation yourself on the real model:

Check it yourselfType the lines after >>>. The lines under them are what Python prints.
>>> import joblib, pandas as pd
>>> FEATURES = ["required_skill_match", "preferred_skill_match", "experience_match", "education_match",
...             "technology_match", "project_relevance", "semantic_similarity"]
>>> model = joblib.load("outputs/model.pkl")
>>> X = pd.read_csv("data/dataset.csv")[FEATURES]

>>> w = model.coef_[0]                 # the seven weights
>>> avg = X.mean()                     # the average applicant
>>> row = X.iloc[1]                    # candidate number 1 (R0001)
>>> contrib = w * (row - avg)          # weight x (value - average)
>>> print(contrib.round(2).to_string())
required_skill_match     0.08
preferred_skill_match   -0.40
experience_match         0.23
education_match          0.14
technology_match        -0.12
project_relevance        0.57
semantic_similarity     -0.03

>>> base = model.intercept_[0] + (w * avg).sum()       # the starting point
>>> print(round(base, 2))
-1.03
>>> print(round(base + contrib.sum(), 2))                     # base + all contributions
-0.57
>>> print(round(model.decision_function(X.iloc[[1]])[0], 2))  # the model's own raw score
-0.57

The last two numbers match, so the contributions really do add up to the model's own score. Here is the same kind of calculation for Arjun Johnson, laid out as a table:

Featurevalueaverageweightcontribution
required_skill_match0.4000.3834.48+0.08
preferred_skill_match0.0000.3261.24-0.40
experience_match1.3330.9870.68+0.23
education_match1.0000.8290.81+0.14
technology_match0.2500.3611.12-0.12
project_relevance0.6670.3882.06+0.57
semantic_similarity0.1090.1660.60-0.03

The average applicant's raw score (the base value) is -1.03, which is about 26% as a probability. Adding the seven contributions (+0.46) gives -0.57, the same raw score as the worked example in chapter 4. The two methods agree, which is a check that our explanation is faithful to the model. This is slide 8's question do SHAP contributions correctly reflect the model's behaviour? Answer: yes, exactly.

Why log-odds?

SHAP values are in the model's raw-score units (log-odds), not in percent, because only in those units do contributions add up cleanly. A +1.0 push is worth more probability near the middle than near the extremes. For reading, only the sign and relative size matter.

Reading the three plots

  • Bar chart (global): for each feature, the average size of its push across everyone, ignoring direction. The longest bar is the feature the model relies on most.
  • Beeswarm (global): one dot per candidate per feature. Position left to right is the push. Colour is the feature value (red high, blue low). If red dots sit on the right for every feature, the model behaves sensibly: high values help.
  • Waterfall (local): for one candidate, start at the base value and step through each feature up or down to the final score.

What SHAP cannot tell you

  • It explains the model, not the world. If the model is wrong, the explanation will faithfully show why it was wrong.
  • It is not causal. “Required skills pushed the score up” does not mean learning a skill will cause a job offer.
  • When features are related to each other (required skills and similarity often move together), credit is shared between them in ways that can look odd.
Remember
  • A regex describes the shape of text. Test it on real samples.
  • Cosine similarity compares word-count arrows. TF-IDF makes rare words count more.
  • SHAP for our model: contribution = weight × (value − average). Base value plus contributions equals the final score.
Chapter 6 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 63 lines

skills.py

A small dictionary-and-helpers file that teaches the program that “ML”, “machine learning” and “Machine Learning” are the same skill.

People write the same skill in many ways. One resume says k8s, another says Kubernetes. A computer compares text letter by letter, so it would treat those as two different skills and wrongly decide the candidate is missing one.

This file fixes that. It converts every spelling to one agreed name. That step is called normalization. Your slides list it as objective 2: identify and normalize candidate and job-related skills.

Analogy

Think of a school register. A student might be called “Rob”, “Robbie” or “Robert” by different friends, but the register holds one official name. ALIASES below is the register: nickname on the left, official name on the right.

Other files import this one, so it is the first file to read. It has three tiny tools: normalize_skill, normalize_skills and mentions.

1"""
2Skill normalization (slide 3, objective 2): map the many ways a candidate can
3write a skill ("ML", "k8s", "Amazon Web Services") onto one canonical name.
4"""
Lines 1–4

Lines 1 to 4 are a docstring: text between triple quotes """. It is a note for humans describing what the file is for. Python reads it but does nothing with it.

“Slide 3, objective 2” points back to your presentation, so a reader can see why this file exists.

5import re

import re borrows a toolbox that comes with Python. re stands for regular expressions, a way of describing text patterns (chapter 5 teaches them). We use it on lines 52 and 62.

The curly brackets { } make a dictionary, which is a list of pairs written key: value, like a phone book (name → number). Here the key is a nickname and the value is the official skill name.

46 "react.js": "react",
47 "nextjs": "next.js",
48}
Lines 42–48

The last pairs: html5, css3, reactjs, react.js and nextjs are folded into their plain names. Line 48 is the closing } that ends the dictionary.

Adding a new alias later is easy: write one more "nickname": "official name", line.

51def normalize_skill(skill: str) -> str:
52 s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", skill.strip().lower())
53 return ALIASES.get(s, s)
Lines 51–53

This is a function: a named recipe you can run many times. def starts the definition.

  • Line 51. normalize_skill is its name. skill: str says it receives one piece of text. -> str says it hands back text. These hints help readers; Python does not enforce them.
  • Line 52. Three steps, read from the inside out. skill.strip() removes spaces at both ends. .lower() makes everything small letters. re.sub(r"\s+", " ", ...) replaces any run of spaces, tabs or line breaks with a single space (\s+ means “one or more whitespace characters”). The result is stored in s.
  • Line 53. ALIASES.get(s, s) looks s up in the dictionary. If it is a known nickname we get the official name. If not, the second s is the fallback, so we get the same text back. return sends the answer out of the function.
You giveYou get
" K8S ""kubernetes"
"Machine Learning""machine learning"
"Rust""rust" (not in the list, so only cleaned)
56def normalize_skills(skills) -> set:
57 return {normalize_skill(s) for s in skills if s and s.strip()}
Lines 56–57

The plural version works on a whole list of skills.

  • Line 57. The curly brackets with a for inside are a set comprehension. Read it aloud: “for each s in skills, if s exists and is not just spaces, put normalize_skill(s) in the set”.
  • A set is a bag with no duplicates and no order. So ["ML", "machine learning"] becomes one item. That matters later, because we count how many skills overlap and a duplicate would inflate the count.
60def mentions(text: str, term: str) -> bool:
61 """Whole-token match, so 'java' does not fire on 'javascript'."""
62 pattern = r"(?<![a-z0-9])" + re.escape(term.lower()) + r"(?![a-z0-9])"
63 return re.search(pattern, text.lower()) is not None
Lines 60–63

This answers “does this text talk about this skill?” and is careful about whole words.

  • Line 61 is the docstring. It gives the key example: java must not match inside javascript.
  • Line 62 builds a search pattern. (?<![a-z0-9]) means “the character before must not be a letter or digit”. (?![a-z0-9]) means the same for the character after. re.escape(...) turns special symbols such as the + in c++ or the / in ci/cd into plain characters. The + signs between pieces simply glue strings together.
  • Line 63. re.search looks for the pattern anywhere in the text (lowercased so capitals do not matter). It returns a match or None. is not None turns that into True or False.

Example: in “I know JavaScript”, the word java is followed by the letter s, so mentions(..., "java") is False. Good.

Remember
  • Normalize means make equal things look equal before comparing.
  • A dictionary stores pairs. A set stores unique items. Both appear everywhere in this project.
  • mentions matches whole words only. That one rule removed a real bug from version 1 of the project.
Try it

Open a terminal in the project folder and run:

cd src
python -c "from skills import normalize_skill, mentions; print(normalize_skill('  K8S ')); print(mentions('I know JavaScript', 'java'))"

You should see kubernetes and then False.

Chapter 7 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 579 lines

author_dataset.py

The dataset factory. It invents 10 job postings and 600 believable fake resumes, and also decides which candidates a pretend recruiter would hire.

A machine learning model learns from examples, so before anything else we need examples. Real resumes are private and hard to get, so this file manufactures them. This is called synthetic data.

Each example needs two parts: the resume itself, and the right answer (was this a good match, yes or no?). The right answer is called the label. Because nobody really hired these fake people, the file includes a small simulated recruiter that makes the call.

Analogy

You are a teacher writing practice exam papers. You invent 600 student answers of different quality and mark each one yourself. Later, a student (the model) practises on those papers and learns what a good answer looks like.

This is the second version of the file. Version 1 had only 100 resumes, and they came in just three fixed quality levels, so the model could cheat by recognising the level instead of judging the skills. Version 2 fixes that with a hidden “quality” number for each resume, extra noise, varied spellings and mismatched pairs. Chapter 16 tells that story in full.

The file has three parts: data lists (lines 32 to 350), small helper functions that each invent one piece of a resume, and a main function that runs everything.

1"""
2Author the synthetic resume-job dataset offline (no Anthropic API calls).
3
4v2 design (replaces the 100-row, tier-templated v1):
5 * Each resume has a continuous latent "fit" q (Beta-distributed), not a
6 discrete strong/medium/weak tier, so skill/experience/education/project
7 signals overlap across the quality range instead of being constant per tier.
8 * Candidates list extra, irrelevant skills and write skills in varied forms
9 ("ML", "k8s", "Amazon Web Services") so skill normalization (slide 3) is
10 actually exercised.
11 * ~30% of resumes are paired with a job outside their own field, giving
12 realistic hard negatives and partial-overlap cases.
13 * Education has a field-of-study dimension, not just degree level.
14 * The ground-truth label is a simulated recruiter decision computed from the
15 candidate's true attributes with a formula that differs from the model's
16 engineered features, plus subjectivity noise and random flips.
17
18Usage:
19 python src/author_dataset.py [--num-resumes 600] [--cross-role-frac 0.3] [--seed 42]
20"""
Lines 1–20

A long docstring that records the design. The key phrases, in plain words:

  • latent fit q. “Latent” means hidden. We give every candidate a secret number q between 0 and 1 for how good they are. A resume is then built from q, but the model never sees q. It only sees the resume.
  • Beta-distributed. A Beta distribution is a recipe for random numbers between 0 and 1 with a chosen shape (many near 1, many near 0.5, and so on).
  • Hard negatives. Some resumes are matched with a job outside their own field (a designer applying to a DevOps role). The model must learn to say no.
  • Ground truth label. The “correct answer” comes from the simulated recruiter.

The Usage lines show how to run the file and which options exist.

Six imports, each a toolbox that ships with Python:

__file__ is the location of this very file. .resolve() turns it into a full address. .parent goes up one folder (to src) and a second .parent goes up again (to the project folder). 278# Education fields: which fields count as relevant / adjacent for each job.
279# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
280_TECH_FIELDS = ["Computer Science", "Software Engineering", "Information Technology", "Computer Engineering"]
281_ADJACENT_STEM = ["Electrical Engineering", "Mechanical Engineering", "Physics", "Mathematics", "Business Analytics"]
