Lines 277–282

Education has two parts: the level (bachelor, master) and the field (Computer Science, Fine Arts). A bachelor's in Fine Arts should not count the same as a bachelor's in Computer Science for a Backend job, so we list which fields are good for which job.

  • 280. _TECH_FIELDS is a list of technology degrees. The leading underscore is a habit meaning “for use inside this file only”.
  • 281. _ADJACENT_STEM: nearby science and engineering fields, only partly useful.
  • 282. UNRELATED_FIELDS: fields that do not help for technical jobs.
284JOB_FIELDS = {
285 "J01": (["Computer Science", "Statistics", "Data Science", "Mathematics"], ["Electrical Engineering", "Physics", "Business Analytics"]),
286 "J02": (_TECH_FIELDS, _ADJACENT_STEM),
287 "J03": (_TECH_FIELDS, _ADJACENT_STEM + ["Graphic Design"]),
288 "J04": (_TECH_FIELDS, _ADJACENT_STEM),
289 "J05": (["Computer Science", "Artificial Intelligence", "Data Science", "Computer Engineering"], ["Statistics", "Mathematics", "Electrical Engineering", "Physics"]),
290 "J06": (None, None), # "any field"
291 "J07": (_TECH_FIELDS, _ADJACENT_STEM),
292 "J08": (_TECH_FIELDS, _ADJACENT_STEM),
293 "J09": (_TECH_FIELDS + ["Data Science"], _ADJACENT_STEM + ["Statistics"]),
294 "J10": (["Design", "Human-Computer Interaction", "Graphic Design", "Cognitive Science"], ["Psychology", "Marketing", "Computer Science"]),
295}
Lines 284–295

JOB_FIELDS maps each job id to a tuple of two lists: (relevant fields, adjacent fields).

  • J02 reuses the two lists from above, so its entry is short.
  • _ADJACENT_STEM + ["Graphic Design"] joins two lists with +, so J03 accepts Graphic Design as an adjacent field too.
  • J06 is (None, None). None means “no value”. Here it means any field is fine for a Product Manager.
296for _job in JOBS:
297 _rel, _adj = JOB_FIELDS[_job["id"]]
298 _job["related_fields"] = _rel
299 _job["adjacent_fields"] = _adj
Lines 296–299

A for loop that visits every job and stores its two lists inside the job dictionary.

  • 297. _rel, _adj = JOB_FIELDS[...] is unpacking: it splits the pair into two variables.
  • 298 to 299. Adds two new keys, related_fields and adjacent_fields, to the job. This is why jobs.json contains them.
301EDU_LABEL = {"associate": "Associate's", "bachelor": "Bachelor's", "master": "Master's", "phd": "PhD"}
302EDU_RANK = {"associate": 2, "bachelor": 3, "master": 4, "phd": 5}
Lines 301–302

Two small lookup dictionaries. EDU_LABEL turns a code word into the polite spelling for the resume text. EDU_RANK turns a degree into a number (associate 2, bachelor 3, master 4, PhD 5) so that code can ask “is this degree lower than that one?” with a simple comparison.

304SOFT_SKILLS = ["communication", "teamwork", "problem solving", "time management", "leadership"]
305FILLER = [
306 "Known for clear communication and reliable delivery in cross-functional teams.",
307 "Comfortable working in fast-paced, collaborative environments.",
308 "Consistently focused on measurable outcomes and continuous improvement.",
309 "Enjoys mentoring teammates and documenting best practices.",
310 "Proactive self-starter who takes ownership of ambiguous problems.",
311 "Passionate about learning new tools and sharing knowledge with the team.",
312]
Lines 304–312

SOFT_SKILLS (communication, teamwork) are real things people write, but they are not in any job's skill list. We add them as noise so resumes look natural and the model must ignore them. FILLER holds sentences that end a resume paragraph, so the 600 resumes do not all finish the same way.

314FIRST_NAMES = [
315 "Ava", "Liam", "Maya", "Noah", "Zara", "Ethan", "Priya", "Lucas", "Sofia", "Daniel",
316 "Aisha", "Mateo", "Hana", "Omar", "Elena", "Kenji", "Leila", "Samuel", "Nina", "Arjun",
317 "Chloe", "Diego", "Fatima", "Gabriel", "Isla", "Jonas", "Kavya", "Tomas", "Yara", "Felix",
318]
319LAST_NAMES = [
320 "Patel", "Kim", "Garcia", "Chen", "Okafor", "Nguyen", "Rossi", "Johnson", "Muller", "Silva",
321 "Khan", "Tanaka", "Ivanov", "Haddad", "Santos", "Larsen", "Mehta", "Dubois", "Cohen", "Reyes",
322]
323NAMES = [f"{f} {l}" for f in FIRST_NAMES for l in LAST_NAMES] # 600 unique names
Lines 314–323

Thirty first names and twenty last names. Line 323 makes every combination:

  • [f"{f} {l}" for f in FIRST_NAMES for l in LAST_NAMES] is a list comprehension with two loops. For each first name, go through each last name and build a full name. 30 × 20 = 600 unique names, one per resume.
  • f"{f} {l}" is an f-string: the f in front lets you place variables inside curly brackets.
325RESUME_TEMPLATES = [
326 "{name} is a {prev_title} professional with {experience_years} years of experience, holding a {education}. "
327 "Core skills include {skills_str}. Hands-on experience with {tech_str}. Recent work: {project_summary} {filler}",
328
329 "{name} brings {experience_years} years of experience, most recently in {prev_title} roles, with a {education}. "
330 "Technical strengths span {skills_str}, alongside practical exposure to {tech_str}. {project_summary} {filler}",
331
332 "With {experience_years} years in the field and a {education}, {name} has developed expertise in "
333 "{skills_str}. Tooling experience includes {tech_str}. {project_summary} {filler}",
334
335 "{name} ({education}) has spent {experience_years} years building skills in {skills_str}, "
336 "complemented by familiarity with {tech_str}. {project_summary} {filler}",
337
338 "{prev_title} with {experience_years} years of experience. {name} holds a {education} and works with "
339 "{tech_str}. Skills: {skills_str}. {project_summary} {filler}",
340
341 "Experienced {prev_title} ({experience_years} years). Education: {education}. {name} has worked across "
342 "{skills_str} and tools such as {tech_str}. {project_summary} {filler}",
343]
Lines 325–343

Six templates for the resume paragraph. Words in curly brackets, such as {name} and {skills_str}, are blanks. Python fills them in later with .format(...) (line 495). Having six sentence shapes stops the text from looking identical.

Each template is built from neighbouring quoted pieces that Python glues together. Notice that every template includes {prev_title}, the person's own field, which is useful to the text-similarity step.

345# Canonical skill -> alternative spellings a real candidate might use.
346ALIAS_DISPLAY = {}
347for _alias, _canon in ALIASES.items():
348 ALIAS_DISPLAY.setdefault(_canon, []).append(_alias)
Lines 345–348

This inverts the alias dictionary. ALIASES goes nickname → official name. We want the opposite: for an official name, which nicknames could a resume use?

  • 347. Loops over every pair.
  • 348. .setdefault(_canon, []) returns the existing list for that official name, or creates an empty one. .append(_alias) adds the nickname to it.

Result: {"machine learning": ["ml"], "kubernetes": ["k8s"], ...}.

350ALL_SKILLS = sorted({s for j in JOBS for s in j["required_skills"] + j["preferred_skills"] + j["technologies"]})
Line 350

Collects every skill used by any job into one sorted list. j["required_skills"] + j["preferred_skills"] + j["technologies"] joins three lists per job; the curly brackets make a set so duplicates vanish; sorted returns a list. We use it to pick distractor skills that a candidate lists but the job does not need.

353def clip01(x):
354 return max(0.0, min(1.0, x))
Lines 353–354

“Clip to 0–1”. min(1.0, x) caps the value at 1, then max(0.0, ...) raises it to at least 0. So the result always stays between 0 and 1. Probabilities must live in that range.

357def write_skill(canon):
358 """Render a canonical skill the way a candidate might actually write it."""
359 options = ALIAS_DISPLAY.get(canon)
360 if options and random.random() < 0.30:
361 return random.choice(options)
362 if random.random() < 0.15:
363 return canon.title()
364 return canon
Lines 357–364

Writes a skill the way a person might, often not in the official form.

  • 359. Looks up the nicknames for this skill. If there are none, options is None.
  • 360 to 361. random.random() gives a number from 0 to 1. If nicknames exist and that number is below 0.30 (a 30% chance), return a random nickname such as k8s.
  • 362 to 363. Otherwise, with a 15% chance, return it capitalised (Python).
  • 364. Otherwise return it unchanged.
367def bernoulli_subset(items, p_mean, spread=0.15):
368 """Include each item independently; the per-resume probability is itself noisy."""
369 p = clip01(random.gauss(p_mean, spread))
370 return [x for x in items if random.random() < p]
Lines 367–370

Decides which items from a list a candidate “has”. Think of flipping a biased coin for each item. A flip like that is called a Bernoulli trial.

  • 369. random.gauss(p_mean, spread) picks a number from a bell curve centred on p_mean. clip01 keeps it between 0 and 1. That number p is this candidate's chance of having each item. Because it is itself random, two candidates with the same q still differ.
  • 370. A list comprehension with a filter: keep x if a fresh random number is below p. Higher p keeps more items.
373def sample_latent_fit(bucket):
374 """Latent 'how good a candidate is for their own field' in [0, 1]."""
375 if bucket == "strong":
376 return random.betavariate(6, 1.8)
377 if bucket == "medium":
378 return random.betavariate(4, 4)
379 return random.betavariate(1.8, 6)
Lines 373–379

Turns a bucket name into the secret quality number q.

random.betavariate(a, b) draws from a Beta distribution. Its average is a / (a + b):

BucketSettingsAverage q
strong(6, 1.8)0.77
medium(4, 4)0.50
weak(1.8, 6)0.23

Only the average is set, not the exact value, so strong and medium candidates overlap. That overlap is what makes the dataset realistic.

382def quality_buckets(n):
383 """Exactly 35% strong / 35% medium / 30% weak, shuffled (stratified per job)."""
384 n_strong, n_medium = round(0.35 * n), round(0.35 * n)
385 buckets = ["strong"] * n_strong + ["medium"] * n_medium + ["weak"] * (n - n_strong - n_medium)
386 random.shuffle(buckets)
387 return buckets
Lines 382–387

Makes sure each job gets the same mix of quality levels.

  • 384. round(0.35 * n) is how many strong and how many medium. Two names are assigned in one line, separated by a comma.
  • 385. ["strong"] * n_strong repeats an item (["strong", "strong", ...]). The three lists are joined with +. The weak count is whatever remains.
  • 386 to 387. random.shuffle mixes the list in place, then it is returned.
Why this exists

Our first attempt picked quality levels purely at random, and by bad luck Data Scientist got far fewer good candidates than the other jobs. Fixing the counts removed that accident.

390def pick_education(persona, q):
391 w_assoc = 0.10 * (1 - q) + 0.02
392 w_master = 0.12 + 0.22 * q
393 w_phd = 0.02 + 0.06 * q
394 w_bach = 1 - w_assoc - w_master - w_phd
395 level = random.choices(["associate", "bachelor", "master", "phd"], weights=[w_assoc, w_bach, w_master, w_phd])[0]
396 rel, adj = JOB_FIELDS[persona["id"]]
397 if rel is None:
398 field = random.choice(["Business Administration", "Economics", "Computer Science", "Marketing", "Psychology", "Engineering"])
399 else:
400 r = random.random()
401 p_rel = 0.30 + 0.65 * q
402 if r < p_rel:
403 field = random.choice(rel)
404 elif r < p_rel + (1 - p_rel) * 0.5:
405 field = random.choice(adj)
406 else:
407 field = random.choice(UNRELATED_FIELDS)
408 return level, field
Lines 390–408

Picks a degree level and field for a candidate. Better candidates (higher q) tend to have more education.

  • 391 to 394. Four weights, one per level. As q rises, the master's and PhD weights grow and the associate weight shrinks. The bachelor weight is whatever is left so the four add up to 1.
  • 395. random.choices(levels, weights=[...]) picks one level, favouring heavier weights. It returns a list, so [0] takes the first item.
  • 396. Gets the relevant and adjacent field lists for this person's own field.
  • 397 to 398. If the list is None (Product Manager, any field), pick any common field.
  • 400 to 407. Otherwise roll a number r. With probability p_rel = 0.30 + 0.65 q the field is relevant. The remaining chance is split in half between adjacent and unrelated fields. Stronger candidates mostly study the right thing.
  • 408. return level, field sends back two values as a pair.
411def pick_projects(persona_id, q):
412 n_total = random.choice([2, 3, 3])
413 n_rel = sum(random.random() < (0.10 + 0.85 * q) for _ in range(n_total))
414 chosen = random.sample(RELEVANT_PROJECTS[persona_id], k=min(n_rel, len(RELEVANT_PROJECTS[persona_id])))
415 chosen += random.sample(UNRELATED_PROJECTS, k=n_total - len(chosen))
416 random.shuffle(chosen)
417 return [{"title": t, "description": d} for t, d in chosen]
Lines 411–417

Chooses the projects shown on a resume.

  • 412. Two or three projects. [2, 3, 3] lists 3 twice, so it is twice as likely.
  • 413. For each project slot, flip a coin with chance 0.10 + 0.85 q of being relevant. sum(...) adds them up. In Python True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the sum counts the relevant ones.
  • 414. random.sample(list, k=...) picks that many different items. min(n_rel, len(...)) guards against asking for more than exist.
  • 415. += adds items to the list: fill the remaining slots with unrelated projects.
  • 416 to 417. Shuffle, then turn each (title, description) pair into a dictionary with those two keys.
420def field_factor(job, field):
421 rel, adj = job.get("related_fields"), job.get("adjacent_fields")
422 if rel is None:
423 return 1.0
424 if field in rel:
425 return 1.0
426 if field in adj:
427 return 0.8
428 return 0.55
Lines 420–428

A multiplier for how well a degree field suits a job: 1.0 for a relevant field, 0.8 for an adjacent one, 0.55 for an unrelated one, and always 1.0 when the job accepts any field (rel is None). It is used by the recruiter on line 456.

431def count_relevant_projects(projects, job):
432 terms = job["required_skills"] + job["technologies"]
433 return sum(
434 any(mentions(p["title"] + " " + p["description"], t) for t in terms) for p in projects
435 )
Lines 431–435

Counts how many of a candidate's projects are relevant to a job.

  • 432. The words to look for: required skills plus technologies.
  • 433 to 435. For each project, any(...) is true if at least one term is mentioned in the title plus description. sum(...) then counts the projects where that was true. mentions is the whole-word check from skills.py.
438def recruiter_decision(cand, job):
439 """
440 Simulated recruiter ground truth, computed from the candidate's *true*
441 attributes. Deliberately NOT the same formula as the model's 7 features:
442 it uses absolute year-gaps, ordinal degree gaps, a hard 'missing too many
443 required skills' penalty, per-recruiter subjectivity, and random flips.
444 The classifier only sees noisy engineered features, so it has to learn an
445 approximation rather than invert a known formula.
446 """
Lines 438–446

The simulated recruiter. The docstring is important, so read it twice.

It marks each candidate good or poor. To keep the experiment honest, it deliberately uses a different formula from the model's seven features. If the recruiter used the same formula, the model could simply copy it and score near 100%, which proves nothing. Instead the model must learn a rough approximation.

447 canon = cand["_canon_skills"]
448 canon_tech = cand["_canon_tech"]
449 req = len(canon & normalize_skills(job["required_skills"])) / len(job["required_skills"])
450 pref = len(canon & normalize_skills(job["preferred_skills"])) / len(job["preferred_skills"])
451 tech = len(canon_tech & normalize_skills(job["technologies"])) / len(job["technologies"])
Lines 447–451
  • 447 to 448. The candidate's true skills and tools, already cleaned. The keys start with an underscore because they are hidden helpers that are deleted before saving (line 565).
  • 449 to 451. Three overlap shares. & between two sets means the items in both. We divide by the number of job skills. If a candidate has 3 of 5 required skills, req is 0.6.
452 exp_term = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-(cand["experience_years"] - job["min_experience"] + 0.5) / 0.8))
Line 452

The experience score is an S-curve (a sigmoid), not a straight ratio. With the job needing M years:

Candidate hasScore
M − 2 years0.13
M − 1 year0.35
M years0.65
M + 1 year0.87

Being a couple of years short hurts a lot; each extra year past the requirement adds less and less. math.exp is the mathematical function e to the power of a number.

454 gap = EDU_RANK[job["education_level"]] - EDU_RANK[cand["_edu_level"]]
455 level_term = 1.0 if gap <= 0 else (0.6 if gap == 1 else 0.3)
456 edu_term = level_term * field_factor(job, cand["_edu_field"])
Lines 454–456
  • 454. How many degree levels short the candidate is (positive means short).
  • 455. A conditional expression: A if condition else B. No gap gives 1.0. One level short gives 0.6. More than one level short gives 0.3. The brackets nest a second choice.
  • 456. Multiply by the field multiplier from lines 420 to 428.
458 proj_term = min(count_relevant_projects(cand["projects"], job) / 2, 1.0)
Line 458

Project score: two relevant projects earn full marks (min(count / 2, 1.0)), one earns half, none earns zero.

460 s = 0.36 * req + 0.07 * pref + 0.13 * tech + 0.17 * exp_term + 0.12 * edu_term + 0.15 * proj_term
Line 460

The recruiter's overall score s is a weighted sum. The weights add up to exactly 1:

PartWeight
Required skills0.36
Experience0.17
Projects0.15
Technologies0.13
Education0.12
Preferred skills0.07

So this recruiter cares most about required skills, a fact the trained model should rediscover.

461 if req < 0.4:
462 s -= 0.12
463 if req >= 0.99 and exp_term > 0.6:
464 s += 0.05
Lines 461–464

Two extra rules that a plain weighted sum cannot express:

  • 461 to 462. If the candidate has fewer than 40% of the required skills, subtract 0.12. A real recruiter rejects such people quickly.
  • 463 to 464. If they have every required skill and decent experience, add 0.05.

s -= 0.12 is shorthand for s = s - 0.12.

465 s += random.gauss(0, 0.07)
Line 465

Adds a small random wobble from a bell curve with average 0 and spread 0.07. That is the recruiter's mood. Two nearly equal candidates can go either way.

466 label = int(s >= LABEL_THRESHOLD)
467 if random.random() < 0.04:
468 label = 1 - label
469 return label, s
Lines 466–469
  • 466. s >= LABEL_THRESHOLD is True or False; int(...) turns it into 1 or 0. This is the label: 1 = good match.
  • 467 to 468. With a 4% chance, flip the answer (1 - label). Real hiring decisions contain inconsistent calls, and this stops the model from reaching a perfect score.
  • 469. Returns both the label and the score.
472def build_resume(idx, persona, job, q, name):
Line 472

The function that builds one whole resume. It receives a counter (idx), the candidate's own field (persona), the job they are paired with (job), their secret quality q, and a name.

473 # Skills / technologies / experience are generated relative to the persona's own field
474 skills = bernoulli_subset(persona["required_skills"], q)
475 skills += bernoulli_subset(persona["preferred_skills"], q * 0.85)
476 technologies = bernoulli_subset(persona["technologies"], q, spread=0.2)
Lines 473–476
  • 473. A reminder: skills come from the candidate's own field, not from the job they are paired with. That is how a mismatched pair arises.
  • 474. Each required skill of their field is kept with probability near q (from bernoulli_subset).
  • 475. Preferred skills are added to the same list with +=, at a slightly lower rate (q * 0.85).
  • 476. Technologies, with a wider spread of 0.2.
477 # Distractors: real candidates list extra skills that are irrelevant (or partly relevant) to this job
478 distractors = random.sample([s for s in ALL_SKILLS if s not in skills], k=random.randint(1, 4))
479 skills += distractors
480 skills += random.sample(SOFT_SKILLS, k=random.randint(0, 2))
481 random.shuffle(skills)
Lines 477–481
  • 478. Distractors: 1 to 4 skills picked from the all-skills list, excluding ones already present. Real candidates list extra things. random.randint(1, 4) picks a whole number from 1 to 4.
  • 479. Add them to the skills.
  • 480. Add 0 to 2 soft skills.
  • 481. Shuffle so the order does not reveal which are which.
483 years = round(persona["min_experience"] * (0.25 + 1.5 * q) + random.gauss(0, 1.1))
484 if random.random() < 0.05:
485 years += 3 # long-tenured outliers
486 years = max(0, years)
Lines 483–486

Years of experience.

  • 483. min_experience * (0.25 + 1.5 q), plus wobble. If a job needs 3 years and q is 0.5, the centre is 3 years. A weak candidate (q 0.2) lands near 1.6 years, a strong one (0.9) near 4.8. random.gauss(0, 1.1) adds a bell-curve wobble and round makes it a whole number.
  • 484 to 485. 5% of people get +3 years, to add a few unusually experienced people.
  • 486. max(0, years) stops a negative number of years.
488 level, field = pick_education(persona, q)
489 education = f"{EDU_LABEL[level]} in {field}"
490 projects = pick_projects(persona["id"], q)
Lines 488–490
  • 488. Calls pick_education and unpacks the two returned values.
  • 489. Builds readable text such as Bachelor's in Statistics from a dictionary lookup and an f-string.
  • 490. Chooses projects.
492 written_skills = [write_skill(s) for s in skills]
493 written_tech = [write_skill(t) for t in technologies]
494 project_summary = " ".join(f"Led \"{p['title']}\": {p['description']}" for p in projects)
Lines 492–494
  • 492 to 493. Turns each clean skill and technology into how a person might write it (sometimes a nickname). Notice the cleaned versions (skills) are kept separately for the recruiter, so the recruiter knows the truth.
  • 494. Builds a sentence for each project, Led "Title": description. The \" inside the f-string is a quote mark that does not end the string. " ".join(...) glues all the sentences together with spaces.
495 resume_text = random.choice(RESUME_TEMPLATES).format(
496 name=name,
497 prev_title=persona["title"],
498 experience_years=years,
499 education=education,
500 skills_str=", ".join(written_skills) if written_skills else "general professional skills",
501 tech_str=", ".join(written_tech) if written_tech else "standard office tooling",
502 project_summary=project_summary,
503 filler=random.choice(FILLER),
504 )
Lines 495–504

Fills in a random template.

  • 495. random.choice(RESUME_TEMPLATES) picks one of the six, and .format( starts filling its blanks.
  • 496 to 499. Fills name, field, years and education. Each is written blank_name=value.
  • 500 to 501. ", ".join(list) makes python, sql, pandas. The part ... if written_skills else "general professional skills" is a safety net for the rare empty list.
  • 502 to 503. Fills the project text and a random closing sentence.
506 cand = {
507 "id": f"R{idx:04d}",
508 "job_id": job["id"],
509 "persona_job_id": persona["id"],
510 "name": name,
511 "skills": written_skills,
512 "experience_years": years,
513 "education": education,
514 "education_level": level,
515 "education_field": field,
516 "technologies": written_tech,
517 "projects": projects,
518 "resume_text": resume_text,
519 "_canon_skills": normalize_skills(skills),
520 "_canon_tech": normalize_skills(technologies),
521 "_edu_level": level,
522 "_edu_field": field,
523 }
Lines 506–523

The finished resume as a dictionary.

  • 507. f"R{idx:04d}" makes ids like R0007. The :04d part means “a whole number padded with zeros to four digits”.
  • 508 to 509. job_id is the job the resume is being compared with. persona_job_id is the field the person actually comes from. They are different for mismatched pairs.
  • 511 to 518. The visible resume content: skills as written, years, education, projects, text.
  • 519 to 522. Hidden helpers for the recruiter (start with an underscore). They hold the true, cleaned skills and the true degree.
524 cand["label"], cand["recruiter_score"] = recruiter_decision(cand, job)
Line 524

Calls the recruiter and stores both answers at once. Writing a, b = function(...) unpacks the two returned values into two dictionary entries: label (0 or 1) and recruiter_score.

525 if persona["id"] != job["id"]:
526 cand["tier"] = "cross-role"
527 else:
528 cand["tier"] = "strong" if q >= 0.7 else ("medium" if q >= 0.4 else "weak")
529 cand["recruiter_score"] = round(cand["recruiter_score"], 4)
530 return cand
Lines 525–530
  • 525 to 526. If the person's own field differs from the job, the tier is cross-role.
  • 527 to 528. Otherwise label the tier by q: 0.7 and above is strong, 0.4 and above is medium, below that is weak. The nested A if x else (B if y else C) is a three-way choice. The tier is only a tag for humans; it is never given to the model.
  • 529. Rounds the score to 4 decimals.
  • 530. Returns the finished resume.
533LABEL_THRESHOLD = 0.55
Line 533

The pass mark: a recruiter score of 0.55 or more means “good match”. We first tried 0.57, which produced 35% good matches; 0.55 gives 37.5%. The functions above read this constant when they run, so it is fine that it appears after them.

536def main():
537 parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
538 parser.add_argument("--num-resumes", type=int, default=600, help="total resume-job pairs (default 600)")
539 parser.add_argument("--cross-role-frac", type=float, default=0.30,
540 help="fraction of resumes evaluated against a job other than their own field")
541 parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
542 args = parser.parse_args()
543 random.seed(args.seed)
Lines 536–543

The main() function runs the whole show.

  • 537. Creates the command-line reader.
  • 538 to 541. Declares three options with defaults: how many resumes (600), what share are mismatched pairs (0.30), and the random seed (42).
  • 542. parse_args() reads what you typed and stores the values on args.
  • 543. random.seed(args.seed) makes randomness repeatable. With the same seed, the same “random” numbers come out in the same order, like shuffling a deck the same way each time. This is why your dataset is identical on every run.
545 if args.num_resumes > len(NAMES):
546 raise SystemExit(f"--num-resumes is capped at {len(NAMES)} (unique names).")
547
548 DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
549 names = random.sample(NAMES, args.num_resumes)
Lines 545–549
  • 545 to 546. A safety check. We only have 600 unique names, so you cannot ask for more. raise SystemExit(...) stops the program and prints that message.
  • 548. Creates the data folder if missing (exist_ok=True means no error if it exists).
  • 549. Picks the names to use, all different.
551 per_job = [args.num_resumes // len(JOBS) + (i < args.num_resumes % len(JOBS)) for i in range(len(JOBS))]
Line 551

How many resumes each job gets. // is whole-number division: 600 // 10 = 60. args.num_resumes % len(JOBS) is the remainder. (i < remainder) is True (1) or False (0), so the first few jobs get one extra when the total does not divide evenly. For 600 every job gets exactly 60.

552 resumes = []
553 idx = 0
554 for persona, n in zip(JOBS, per_job):
555 for bucket in quality_buckets(n):
556 job = persona
557 if random.random() < args.cross_role_frac:
558 job = random.choice([j for j in JOBS if j["id"] != persona["id"]])
559 resumes.append(build_resume(idx, persona, job, sample_latent_fit(bucket), names[idx]))
560 idx += 1
Lines 552–560

The main loop.

  • 552 to 553. An empty list for the results and a counter idx starting at 0.
  • 554. zip(JOBS, per_job) pairs each job with its count. The loop visits one job at a time.
  • 555. For each quality bucket assigned to that job:
  • 556. By default, the resume is compared with its own job.
  • 557 to 558. But 30% of the time, swap in a random other job. The inner list comprehension builds all jobs except the person's own.
  • 559. Builds the resume and adds it to the list with .append.
  • 560. Increase the counter by one.
561 random.shuffle(resumes)
562 for new_idx, r in enumerate(resumes): # re-number after shuffle so ids are in file order
563 r["id"] = f"R{new_idx:04d}"
564 for r in resumes:
565 for k in [k for k in r if k.startswith("_")]:
566 del r[k]
Lines 561–566
  • 561. Shuffles all 600 so jobs are mixed, not in blocks.
  • 562 to 563. enumerate gives a counter with each item. The ids are rewritten in the shuffled order so R0000 is first in the file.
  • 564 to 566. For every resume, delete the hidden helper keys. The list comprehension on line 565 first collects the keys that start with _, and then del removes them. Collecting first is needed because you must not change a dictionary while looping over it.
568 with open(DATA_DIR / "jobs.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
569 json.dump(JOBS, f, indent=2)
570 with open(DATA_DIR / "resumes.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
571 json.dump(resumes, f, indent=2)
Lines 568–571

Saves the results. with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: opens a file for writing and closes it automatically when the block ends. json.dump(JOBS, f, indent=2) writes the data as text, with neat 2-space indentation so you can read it. Two files result: jobs.json and resumes.json.

573 print(f"Wrote {len(JOBS)} jobs and {len(resumes)} resumes to {DATA_DIR}")
574 print("Tier distribution:", dict(Counter(r["tier"] for r in resumes)))

Lines 573–575

Prints a summary so you can check the run. Counter(...) counts the tiers. sum(r['label'] for r in resumes) adds up the 1s, giving the number of good matches (about 225 of 600).

578if __name__ == "__main__":
579 main()
Lines 578–579

The standard Python ending: if __name__ == "__main__": means “only run main() if this file was started directly”. If another file merely imports this one, nothing runs. You will see this ending in nearly every script.

Remember
  • A model needs examples and a label for each. Here the label is a simulated recruiter's decision.
  • q is a hidden quality score. Resumes are built from it, but the model never sees it.
  • Randomness is repeatable because of the seed.
  • The recruiter uses a different formula from the model on purpose, so the model has real work to do.
Honest limit

The labels come from a simulation we wrote, not from real hiring. The model will score well if it recovers our simulated recruiter's tastes. That says nothing about how real companies decide.

Try it

Generate a small dataset with another seed and open the result:

python src/author_dataset.py --num-resumes 50 --seed 7

Open data/resumes.json and read a few resumes. This overwrites the data files, so afterwards run python src/author_dataset.py with no options to restore the standard 600-resume dataset, then re-run the later steps.

Chapter 8 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 186 lines

feature_engineering.py

The translator. It turns each resume and job (words) into seven numbers between 0 and 1.5, because a model can only learn from numbers.

A computer cannot learn from the sentence “Arjun knows Python and SQL”. It can learn from numbers such as 0.4. This file converts every resume-and-job pair into seven numbers. Each number answers one question a recruiter would ask. These numbers are called features.

FeatureThe question it answers
required_skill_matchWhat share of the must-have skills does this person have?
preferred_skill_matchWhat share of the nice-to-have skills?
experience_matchYears of experience compared with the years required.
education_matchDoes their degree level and field meet the requirement?
technology_matchWhat share of the job's tools do they list?
project_relevanceWhat share of their projects relate to this job?
semantic_similarityDoes the resume text sound like the job text?
Analogy

A doctor cannot feed “the patient looks unwell” into a machine. She measures temperature, pulse and blood pressure. Those numbers are the patient's features. This file takes the same measurements from a resume.

The file also joins the pieces into a table, data/dataset.csv, with one row per resume-job pair: the seven features plus the right answer (the label). Here is our running example, Arjun Johnson, compared with the Data Engineer job:

SourceWhat it says
ResumeSkills: python, machine learning, Html, sql, pandas, api testing, test automation framework, google cloud platform, statistics, dl
Tools: python, spark
Experience: 4 years
Education: Bachelor's in Computer Science
Projects: Sales Forecasting Pipeline; Home Renovation Project; A/B Test Analysis Framework
Job (Data Engineer)Must have: python, sql, etl, spark, data pipelines

Notice the resume writes Html, dl and google cloud platform in odd forms. Normalization (the previous file) cleans them before any comparison. Here only python and sql appear among the job's five must-haves, so the required-skill number is 2 out of 5 = 0.4. The seven numbers for this row, as stored in the dataset:

FeatureValue
required_skill_match0.400
preferred_skill_match0.000
experience_match1.333
education_match1.000
technology_match0.250
project_relevance0.667
semantic_similarity0.109

  • numpy handles numbers and random values quickly. Here it is only used in a fallback path (lines 151 to 153).

Line 18

Line 20

Finds the data folder, exactly as in the previous file: this file's folder, up two levels, then data.

22EDU_RANK = {"associate": 2, "bachelor": 3, "master": 4, "phd": 5}
23EDU_LEVELS = [
24 (r"phd|doctor", 5),
25 (r"master", 4),
26 (r"bachelor", 3),
27 (r"associate", 2),
28 (r"high school", 1),
29]
Lines 22–29

Two ways to turn a degree into a number.

  • 22. EDU_RANK maps the code words to ranks: associate 2, bachelor 3, master 4, PhD 5.
  • 23 to 29. EDU_LEVELS is a list of pairs: a text pattern and a rank. This is for resumes that only have a sentence like “Master of Science”. The r"..." is a raw string, where backslashes are left alone, which is the habit for patterns. The | in phd|doctor means “or”. The list is ordered from the highest degree down, which matters on line 34.
32def education_level(text: str) -> int:
33 text = text.lower()
34 for pattern, level in EDU_LEVELS:
35 if re.search(pattern, text):
36 return level
37 return 3 # default to bachelor's-equivalent when unclear
Lines 32–37

Reads a degree's rank from free text.

  • 33. Lowercases the text so capital letters do not matter.
  • 34 to 36. Loops through the patterns from highest to lowest. At the first pattern found in the text, return level ends the function with that number. Highest-first means “Master's and Bachelor's” scores as a master's.
  • 37. If nothing matched, assume a bachelor's (3). After # is a comment explaining the choice.
40def skill_overlap_ratio(candidate_skills: list, job_skills: list) -> float:
41 """Share of the job's skills the candidate has, after skill normalization (slide 3)."""
42 if not job_skills:
43 return 0.0
44 cand = normalize_skills(candidate_skills)
45 job = normalize_skills(job_skills)
46 return len(cand & job) / len(job)
Lines 40–46

The workhorse for four of the seven features: what share of the job's skills does the candidate have?

  • 42 to 43. If the job lists no skills, return 0.0. This guard prevents dividing by zero on line 46.
  • 44 to 45. Clean both lists with normalize_skills so “k8s” equals “kubernetes”. Each becomes a set.
  • 46. cand & job is the intersection: the skills in both sets. len(...) counts them. Divide by how many skills the job lists.

Example. The job needs {python, sql, pandas, statistics, machine learning}. The candidate has {python, sql, excel}. The overlap is 2 skills out of 5, so the result is 2 / 5 = 0.4.

Notice we divide by the job's list, so extra skills never lower the score. Having Excel does not hurt.

49def _field_in(field: str, options: list) -> bool:
50 """Case-insensitive; also tolerates 'Computer Science & Engineering' vs 'Computer Science'."""
51 f = field.strip().lower()
52 return any(f == o.lower() or o.lower() in f for o in options)
Lines 49–52

Decides whether a study field counts as one of a list of options.

  • 51. Cleans the field to lowercase without extra spaces.
  • 52. any(...) is true if at least one option matches. An option matches if the texts are equal, or if the option appears inside the field. That second test helps a resume that says “Computer Science & Engineering” match the option “Computer Science”.

A name starting with _ signals a helper for this file only.

55def education_compatibility(resume: dict, job: dict) -> float:
56 """Degree level vs. requirement, discounted when the field of study is unrelated."""
57 cand_edu = EDU_RANK.get(resume.get("education_level")) or education_level(resume["education"])
58 req_edu = EDU_RANK.get(job.get("education_level")) or education_level(job["education"])
59 level_score = 1.0 if cand_edu >= req_edu else cand_edu / req_edu
60
61 related, adjacent = job.get("related_fields"), job.get("adjacent_fields")
62 field = resume.get("education_field")
63 if related is None or field is None:
64 return level_score
65 if _field_in(field, related):
66 factor = 1.0
67 elif _field_in(field, adjacent or []):
68 factor = 0.8
69 else:
70 factor = 0.55
71 return level_score * factor
Lines 55–71

Scores education from 0 to 1, using the degree level and the field.

  • 57. The candidate's rank. resume.get("education_level") returns the value, or None if the resume lacks it. EDU_RANK.get(...) turns it into a number. A or B means “use A, and if A is empty or None, use B”. So if no level is stored, we guess it from the sentence using education_level.
  • 58. The same for the job's required level.
  • 59. If the candidate's rank meets or beats the requirement, the level score is 1.0. Otherwise it is the ratio. Example: associate (2) for a bachelor's job (3) gives 2 / 3 = 0.67.
  • 61 to 62. Fetches the lists of relevant and adjacent fields and the candidate's field.
  • 63 to 64. If the job accepts any field or the resume lacks one, return the level score alone.
  • 65 to 70. The multiplier: 1.0 for a relevant field, 0.8 for an adjacent one, 0.55 for an unrelated one.
  • 71. Final score = level score × field multiplier. A bachelor's in Fine Arts for a tech job scores 1.0 × 0.55.
74def project_relevance(projects: list, keywords: list) -> float:
75 if not projects:
76 return 0.0
77 kw = {k.lower() for k in keywords}
78 hits = 0
79 for p in projects:
80 text = p.get("title", "") + " " + p.get("description", "")
81 if any(mentions(text, k) for k in kw): # whole-token match: "java" != "javascript"
82 hits += 1
83 return hits / len(projects)
Lines 74–83

What share of a candidate's projects mention something the job needs?

  • 75 to 76. No projects means 0.0.
  • 77. A set of the job's keywords, in lowercase.
  • 78. hits counts the relevant projects, starting at zero.
  • 79 to 80. For each project, glue its title and description into one text. p.get("title", "") returns an empty string if the title is missing, instead of crashing.
  • 81 to 82. any(...) checks whether at least one keyword appears as a whole word. If so, add 1 to hits.
  • 83. Relevant projects divided by all projects. Three projects with two relevant gives 0.67.
86def compute_features(resume: dict, job: dict, semantic_similarity: float) -> dict:
87 """The 7 slide-5 features for one resume against one job. Shared by training and the app."""
88 return {
89 "required_skill_match": skill_overlap_ratio(resume["skills"], job["required_skills"]),
90 "preferred_skill_match": skill_overlap_ratio(resume["skills"], job["preferred_skills"]),
91 "experience_match": (
92 min(resume["experience_years"] / job["min_experience"], 1.5) if job["min_experience"] else 1.0
93 ),
94 "education_match": education_compatibility(resume, job),
95 "technology_match": skill_overlap_ratio(resume["technologies"], job["technologies"]),
96 "project_relevance": project_relevance(
97 resume["projects"], job["required_skills"] + job["technologies"]
98 ),
99 "semantic_similarity": semantic_similarity,
100 }
Lines 86–100

The central function: one resume + one job + one similarity number in, seven features out. It is used both here for training and later by the app, so the model always sees features calculated the same way.

  • 88. Returns a dictionary. Its keys are the feature names.
  • 89. required_skill_match: overlap with the job's required skills.
  • 90. preferred_skill_match: overlap with the preferred skills.
  • 91 to 93. experience_match is min(years / years_required, 1.5). A candidate with exactly the needed years scores 1.0; one with 4.5 years for a 3-year job is capped at 1.5, because extra years help with diminishing returns. If the job's requirement is 0, the part after else gives 1.0, avoiding division by zero. The whole thing is a conditional expression, A if condition else B.
  • 94. education_match from the function above.
  • 95. technology_match: the candidate's tools against the job's tools.
  • 96 to 98. project_relevance: projects checked against the job's required skills plus its technologies (two lists joined with +).
  • 99. semantic_similarity is passed in, because it needs the text-similarity machinery set up in build_dataset.
103def build_dataset() -> pd.DataFrame:
104 with open(DATA_DIR / "jobs.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
105 jobs = {j["id"]: j for j in json.load(f)}
106 with open(DATA_DIR / "resumes.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
107 resumes = json.load(f)
Lines 103–107

Starts the function that builds the whole table, and loads the two data files.

  • 104 to 105. with open(...) as f opens the file and closes it afterwards. json.load(f) reads it into Python lists and dictionaries. The curly-bracket expression {j["id"]: j for j in ...} is a dictionary comprehension: it builds a lookup table from job id to job, so jobs["J05"] returns that job.
  • 106 to 107. Loads the resumes as a plain list.
109 # Semantic similarity via TF-IDF over resume_text + job description_text
110 job_ids = list(jobs.keys())
111 job_texts = [jobs[jid]["description_text"] for jid in job_ids]
112 resume_texts = [r["resume_text"] for r in resumes]
113 vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
114 build_dataset.vectorizer = vectorizer # saved by main() so the app scores similarity on the training scale
115 all_vecs = vectorizer.fit_transform(job_texts + resume_texts)
116 job_vecs = all_vecs[: len(job_texts)]
117 resume_vecs = all_vecs[len(job_texts):]
118 job_vec_by_id = {jid: job_vecs[i] for i, jid in enumerate(job_ids)}
Lines 109–118

Sets up the text-similarity machinery. Chapter 5 teaches how TF-IDF works; here is what each line does.

  • 110. The list of job ids.
  • 111 to 112. The job descriptions as one list of texts, and the resume texts as another.
  • 113. Creates a TF-IDF vectorizer. stop_words="english" tells it to ignore very common words like “the” and “and”.
  • 114. Attaches the vectorizer to the function as build_dataset.vectorizer, a place to keep it so main() can save it. The app needs this exact vectorizer later, so that similarity numbers sit on the same scale the model trained on.
  • 115. fit_transform does two things. Fit: learn the vocabulary of all texts and how rare each word is. Transform: turn every text into a list of numbers. We pass jobs and resumes together (+ joins the lists). The result is a big table with one row per text.
  • 116 to 117. Slices that table. The first rows belong to jobs, the rest to resumes. [: n] means “up to n” and [n:] means “from n onward”.
  • 118. A lookup from job id to that job's row of numbers. enumerate supplies the position i of each id.

121 for i, r in enumerate(resumes):
122 job = jobs[r["job_id"]]
123
124 feats = compute_features(
125 r, job, float(cosine_similarity(resume_vecs[i], job_vec_by_id[r["job_id"]])[0, 0])
126 )

Now the loop that produces one table row per resume.

  • 122. Finds the job this resume is being compared with.
  • 124 to 126. Calls compute_features with an extra argument: the similarity. cosine_similarity(a, b) returns a small table, so [0, 0] picks the one number we want. float(...) makes it a normal number.

Chapter 9 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 78 lines

train_model.py

The learning step. It shows the model 450 solved examples, then quizzes it on 150 it has never seen and records the marks.

This short file is the heart of machine learning, and it is only about 50 lines. It does four things:

  1. Reads the table from the previous step.
  2. Splits it into a practice set (to learn from) and an exam set (to be tested on).
  3. Lets the model learn from the practice set.
  4. Marks the model on the exam set and saves everything.
Analogy

A student prepares for an exam with practice papers. If the real exam used the same papers, a high mark would only prove memory. So a teacher hides some papers and uses those for the exam. The same idea applies here: never test a model on examples it practised on.

The model we use is Logistic Regression. Chapter 4 explains it with a live demo. For now: it gives each of the seven features a weight (how much it matters), adds them up, and turns the total into a probability between 0 and 1.

Our results, so you know what to expect: on the 150 exam rows the model scored 0.907 accuracy. Using a steadier method (5-fold cross-validation, explained below) it scored 0.932, give or take 0.013.

Splits the data into practice and exam sets. train_test_split returns four things, unpacked into four names:

  • X_train, y_train: the practice questions and their answers (450 rows).
  • X_test, y_test: the exam questions and the hidden answers (150 rows).

The settings:

  • test_size=0.25: one quarter goes to the exam.
  • random_state=42: makes the shuffle repeatable, so you get the same split each run.
  • stratify=y: keep the same share of good matches (about 37%) in both sets. Without it, bad luck could put most good matches in one set and make the exam unfair.
40 model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
41 model.fit(X_train, y_train)
Lines 40–41
  • 40. Creates an untrained Logistic Regression. max_iter=1000 gives its learning routine up to 1000 tries to settle on good weights. It normally needs far fewer; the cap just prevents a stuck loop.
  • 41. model.fit(X_train, y_train) is the learning. The model looks at the 450 practice rows and their answers and adjusts its seven weights until its predictions match the answers as closely as it can. It takes a fraction of a second.
43 y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
Line 43

The exam. model.predict(X_test) gives the model the 150 exam questions without the answers. It returns its guesses, 0 or 1 for each. We compare them with the true answers (y_test) in the next lines.

44 cv = cross_validate(
45 LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), X, y,
46 cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42),
47 scoring=["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"],
48 )
Lines 44–48

Cross-validation: a steadier way to test. One 150-row exam can be unlucky. So we repeat the whole practice-and-exam cycle five times, each time hiding a different fifth of the data, and average the five marks.

  • 45. A fresh, untrained model, plus the full X and y.
  • 46. StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42): split into 5 parts ("folds"), shuffled, keeping the good/poor balance in each.
  • 47. Which measurements to record each time.

The result cv holds five numbers for every measurement. The spread between them (the standard deviation, "std") tells you how stable the model is. Our version-1 data had folds ranging from 0.75 to 1.00, a sign of too little data.

49 metrics = {
50 "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
51 "precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
52 "recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
53 "f1_score": f1_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
54 "roc_auc": roc_auc_score(y_test, model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]),
55 "confusion_matrix": confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred).tolist(),
Lines 49–55

Builds a dictionary of results, using four standard marks. Here are plain definitions, each with our real numbers from the exam:

  • 50. accuracy: the share of all answers that were right. (0.907)
  • 51. precision: when the model says “good match”, how often is it right? (0.875)
  • 52. recall: of all the truly good matches, how many did the model find? (0.875)
  • 53. f1_score: one number that balances precision and recall. (0.875)
  • 54. roc_auc: how well the model ranks good above poor, ignoring any cut-off. 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing. (0.956). predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] gives the probabilities; [:, 1] takes the second column, the probability of “good”.
  • 55. confusion_matrix: the table of right and wrong answers. .tolist() turns it into a plain list that JSON can store.

zero_division=0 just says “if a calculation would divide by zero, answer 0 instead of crashing”.

56 "n_train": len(X_train),
57 "n_test": len(X_test),
58 # 5-fold CV over the full dataset: a steadier estimate than one hold-out split
59 "cv_5fold": {
60 name: {"mean": float(cv[f"test_{name}"].mean()), "std": float(cv[f"test_{name}"].std())}
61 for name in ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1", "roc_auc"]
62 },
63 "coefficients": dict(zip(FEATURES, map(float, model.coef_[0]))),
64 }
Lines 56–64
  • 56 to 57. How many rows were used to learn and to test.
  • 58. A comment: the cross-validation average is a more reliable estimate than a single split.
  • 59 to 62. For each measurement name, compute the mean (average of five marks) and std (their spread). The curly-bracket expression is a dictionary comprehension. cv[f"test_{name}"] looks up the five marks, since scikit-learn names them test_accuracy and so on.
  • 63. Saves the learned weights. model.coef_[0] holds one number per feature. zip(FEATURES, ...) pairs each name with its number, and dict(...) turns the pairs into a dictionary. map(float, ...) converts each to a plain number, because JSON cannot store the special number type scikit-learn uses.
66 print(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2))
Line 66

Prints the results. json.dumps(metrics, indent=2) converts the dictionary to nicely indented text.

68 joblib.dump(model, OUT_DIR / "model.pkl")
69 X_test.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "X_test.csv", index=False)
70 y_test.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "y_test.csv", index=False)
71 with open(OUT_DIR / "metrics.json", "w") as f:
72 json.dump(metrics, f, indent=2)
Lines 68–72

Saves everything for later steps.

  • 68. joblib.dump(model, ...) saves the trained model to model.pkl. This is the file the app loads. Training takes about a second; loading it later is instant.
  • 69 to 70. Saves the exam questions and answers as CSV files, so the SHAP step can explain exactly those rows.
  • 71 to 72. Writes the metrics to metrics.json.
74 print(f"\nSaved model to {OUT_DIR / 'model.pkl'}")
Line 74

Prints where the model was saved. \n starts a new line, and OUT_DIR / 'model.pkl' builds the file path.

77if __name__ == "__main__":
78 main()
Lines 77–78

The standard guard: run main() only when the file is started directly. This also lets matcher.py import FEATURES from this file without starting a training run.

Remember
  • Train on one part of the data, test on another that the model has never seen.
  • fit is learning. predict is guessing. Metrics compare the guesses with the truth.
  • One exam can be unlucky. Cross-validation averages five.
  • A saved model.pkl is just the seven weights and one starting number, which is why it is tiny and fast.
Try it 
python src/train_model.py

Open outputs/metrics.json. Find coefficients: the largest number belongs to the feature the model trusts most. It should be required_skill_match. That matches how our simulated recruiter was built (chapter 7).

Chapter 10 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 85 lines

explain_shap.py

The “why” step. For every candidate in the exam set it works out how much each of the seven features pushed the score up or down, and draws pictures of it.

A model that says “82% match” and nothing else is a black box. A recruiter cannot trust it, and a candidate cannot learn from it. Your whole project exists to fix this: prediction + explanation = trust.

The tool for the job is SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). It answers: of this candidate's final score, how much credit or blame does each feature deserve?

Analogy

Seven friends run a stall and make a profit. How do you split it fairly? Some friends brought more customers, and one spent too much on stock. Game theory has a fair method (named after Lloyd Shapley) that credits each friend for what they added. SHAP uses the same method, with the seven features as the friends and the final score as the profit.

For a linear model like ours the sum is simple. Each feature's contribution is its weight × (this candidate's value − the average value). Suppose the weight of a feature is 4.48 and the average applicant scores 0.5 on it. A candidate scoring 1.0 gets 4.48 × (1.0 − 0.5) = +2.24, which pushes toward “good”. A candidate scoring 0.0 gets 4.48 × (0 − 0.5) = −2.24, which pushes toward “poor”.

These contributions are measured in log-odds, the raw score the model computes before squeezing it into 0–1. You do not need the maths. Just remember: positive means pushes toward a good match, negative means pushes toward a poor match, and all contributions plus the starting value add up exactly to the final score. We checked: the error is about 3 in a quadrillion.

1"""
2SHAP explainability for the trained Logistic Regression model (slides 6-7).
3
4Produces:
5 - outputs/shap_summary_global.png : global feature importance (bar)
6 - outputs/shap_beeswarm_global.png : global SHAP distribution
7 - outputs/shap_local_example.png : local waterfall for one test case
8 - outputs/shap_explanations.json : per-feature contributions for every
9 test-set example (strong/negative
10 factors per candidate, slide 7)
11"""
Lines 1–11

The docstring lists the four things this file produces: two global pictures (which features matter overall), one local picture (why one candidate scored what they did), and a JSON file with every test candidate's positive and negative factors.

Global explanation means “across everyone”. Local means “for this one person”. Slide 7 of your deck has both.

Builds the explanation record for this candidate.

Chapter 11 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 165 lines

report_candidate.py

The storyteller. It turns one candidate's numbers into the slide 7 report: a probability, the good factors, the bad factors, and a sentence a human can read.

SHAP gives numbers such as required_skill_match: +1.35. That is useful to a data scientist but not to a recruiter. This file converts those numbers into words and prints a tidy report, the “Example Prediction” on your slide 7.

It has two jobs. First, it holds the wording tables (a friendly label and a phrase for each feature). The app reuses these. Second, it has a command-line tool you can run to see the report for any one candidate.

Analogy

A weather station records temperature and wind speed. The forecaster on television says “it will be a chilly, breezy evening”. This file is the forecaster.

74def narrative(name, title, prob, pos_factors, neg_factors):
Line 74

The function that writes the plain-English sentence. It receives the candidate's name, the job title, the probability, and two lists: features that helped (pos_factors) and features that hurt (neg_factors).

75 """Plain-language explanation. Drivers are the factors pushing in the direction of the prediction."""
76 strong = prob >= 0.5
77 label = "a strong match" if strong else "a weak match"
78 sentence = f"{name} is predicted to be {label} for the {title} role ({prob*100:.0f}% match probability)"
Lines 75–78
  • 75. The docstring states the rule: the “drivers” of a sentence must be the factors pushing in the same direction as the prediction.
  • 76. strong = prob >= 0.5 stores True or False. A probability of 0.5 or more means “good match”.
  • 77. Picks the words “a strong match” or “a weak match” with a conditional expression.
  • 78. Starts the sentence. In the f-string, {prob*100:.0f} multiplies by 100 to get a percentage and shows it with 0 decimals, so 0.78 prints as 78.
79 drivers, drivers_phrases = (pos_factors, POSITIVE_PHRASES) if strong else (neg_factors, NEGATIVE_PHRASES)
80 offsets, offsets_phrases = (neg_factors, NEGATIVE_PHRASES) if strong else (pos_factors, POSITIVE_PHRASES)
Lines 79–80

Chooses which factors drive the sentence and which offset it. Each line picks a pair at once (the list of factors and the matching phrase table):

  • 79. If the prediction is strong, the drivers are the helpful factors; if weak, the drivers are the harmful ones.
  • 80. The offsets are the opposite group.
A real bug we fixed

The first version always used the helpful factors as drivers. A candidate predicted weak was described as “mainly driven by relevant projects”, which is backwards. Explanations that say the wrong thing are worse than none.

81 if drivers:
82 sentence += ", mainly because of " + " and ".join(drivers_phrases[f] for f in drivers[:2])
83 sentence += "."
Lines 81–83
  • 81 to 82. If there are any drivers, add “, mainly because of ” and the first two phrases joined with “ and ”. drivers[:2] means the first two items. " and ".join(...) glues phrases together with that word between them.
  • 83. Ends the sentence with a full stop.
84 if offsets:
85 verb = "held back somewhat by" if strong else "partly offset by"
86 sentence += f" This is {verb} {offsets_phrases[offsets[0]]}."
87 return sentence
Lines 84–87
  • 84 to 86. If any factor pulls the other way, add one more sentence: “This is held back somewhat by ...” for a strong match, or “This is partly offset by ...” for a weak one. It names the single biggest opposing factor, offsets[0].
  • 87. Returns the finished sentence.

120 print(" STRONG POSITIVE FACTORS")
121 if pos:
122 for f, v in pos:
123 print(f" + {FEATURE_LABELS[f]:<32} contribution: +{v:.3f}")
124 else:
125 print(" (none)")

129 for f, v in neg:
130 print(f" - {FEATURE_LABELS[f]:<32} contribution: {v:.3f}")
131 else:
132 print(" (none)")
133 print("-" * w)
Lines 120–133

  • 124 to 125. Otherwise print “(none)”. else pairs with the if above it.
  • 127 to 132. The same for harmful factors.

135 print(" " + narrative(
136 resume["name"], job["title"], prob,
137 [f for f, _ in pos], [f for f, _ in neg],
138 ))
139 print("=" * w)

Remember
  • A good explanation is a sentence, not a number.
  • Phrases are chosen from two tables, one for helpful factors and one for harmful ones.
  • A conditional expression, A if condition else B, appears constantly. Read it as a choice.
  • Always check your explanations say the right thing. We caught a backwards sentence only by reading real output.
Try it

python src/report_candidate.py --random

Run --random three times. For each, does the final sentence agree with the verdict above it?

Chapter 12 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 365 lines

resume_parser.py

The reader. It opens a PDF, Word or text resume, finds the skills, years, degree and projects inside the messy text, and returns the same tidy record the model was trained on.

Everything so far used structured data: neat lists, already separated into skills, years and so on. A real resume is not like that. It is a file with a name at the top, headings, bullet points and dates, laid out however its author liked. To score it, we must first extract the facts. This is called parsing.

There are two ways to build a parser. One uses an AI language model that “reads” the resume. The other uses rules: patterns and word lists. We use rules. They are free, instant, repeatable, and easy to inspect line by line, which suits a learning project. The cost is that rules miss unusual layouts, so the parser also returns warnings saying what it could not find.

Analogy

Imagine a mail clerk who must fill a form from a customer's letter. He looks for the name at the top, a heading that says “Education”, dates like “2019 to 2021”, and words from a list of known skills. If the letter has no education heading, he writes a note on the form saying so. That is this file.

The steps, in order, with the function that does each:

Extract textextract_text→Clean_clean→Split into sectionssplit_sections→Find factsdetect_skills, years, education, projects→One recordparse_resume

A real result. Parsing the sample file Rishab.docx returned: name Rishab, 2.2 years of experience (from the dates “Aug 2024 – Present”), education Bachelor's in Information Technology, one project, and the skills data analysis, data visualization, excel, power bi, python, sql.

This chapter uses regular expressions heavily. If they are new to you, read the regex section of chapter 5 first, then come back. Each pattern below is explained piece by piece.

1"""
2Resume parsing: turn an uploaded PDF / DOCX / TXT resume into the same
3structured record the model was trained on (skills, technologies, years of
4experience, education level + field, projects, full text).
5
6This is a rule-based parser (regex + vocabularies), not an LLM, so it is
7fast, free and deterministic -- but it will miss unusual layouts. Every parse
8returns `warnings` describing anything it could not find, and the app shows them.
9"""
Lines 1–9

The docstring states the design choice: rule-based, not an AI model, which makes it fast, free and predictable. It also promises that every parse returns warnings, which the app displays under the candidate.
