44# Short or everyday-English aliases that would create false positives when scanning free text.
45AMBIGUOUS_ALIASES = {"spring", "torch", "dl", "ts", "stats"}
Lines 44–45

Some nicknames in our alias list are dangerous in free text. “spring” is a season, “torch” is a flashlight, “ts” and “dl” are tiny, “stats” is everyday English. If we searched resumes for them we would find skills that are not there. So we list them here and skip them when scanning text.

47ALIAS_VARIANTS = {}
48for _alias, _canon in ALIASES.items():
49 if _alias not in AMBIGUOUS_ALIASES:
50 ALIAS_VARIANTS.setdefault(_canon, []).append(_alias)
Lines 47–50

Builds the nickname table the parser may use, as in author_dataset.py, but skipping the dangerous ones.

  • 48. Loop over every nickname and its official name.
  • 49. if _alias not in AMBIGUOUS_ALIASES keeps only safe nicknames.
  • 50. .setdefault(_canon, []).append(_alias) adds the nickname to that skill's list, creating the list first if needed.
52KNOWN_FIELDS = [
53 "Computer Science", "Software Engineering", "Information Technology", "Computer Engineering",
54 "Artificial Intelligence", "Data Science", "Statistics", "Mathematics", "Electrical Engineering",
55 "Mechanical Engineering", "Physics", "Business Analytics", "Business Administration", "Economics",
56 "Human-Computer Interaction", "Graphic Design", "Cognitive Science", "Psychology", "Marketing",
57 "Fine Arts", "History", "Hospitality Management", "Design", "Engineering",
58]
Lines 52–58

KNOWN_FIELDS: the study subjects the parser recognises (Computer Science, Statistics, Fine Arts and so on). When we read “B.Sc. in Statistics” we find “Statistics” by looking for these.

60DEGREE_PATTERNS = [ # (level, regex) -- checked highest level first
61 ("phd", r"\bph\.?\s?d\b|\bdoctorate\b|\bdoctor of philosophy\b"),
62 ("master", r"\bmaster'?s?\b|\bm\.?\s?sc\b|\bm\.?\s?tech\b|\bm\.?\s?s\b(?=[\s.,]|$)|\bmba\b|\bm\.?\s?eng\b|\bm\.?\s?e\b(?=[\s.,]|$)"),
63 ("bachelor", r"\bbachelor'?s?\b|\bb\.?\s?sc\b|\bb\.?\s?tech\b|\bb\.?\s?s\b(?=[\s.,]|$)|\bb\.?\s?a\b(?=[\s.,]|$)|\bb\.?\s?e\b(?=[\s.,]|$)|\bundergraduate\b|\bb\.?\s?eng\b"),
64 ("associate", r"\bassociate'?s?\b|\bdiploma\b"),
65]
Lines 60–65

DEGREE_PATTERNS is a list of pairs: a level and a regular expression that finds it. The comment says highest first, because a resume often lists both a Master's and a Bachelor's and we want the higher one.

Reading the patterns:

  • \b means a word edge, so \bmba\b matches “MBA” but not “embark”.
  • ph\.?\s?d matches PhD, Ph.D and Ph. D. The \. is a literal dot, ? means “optional”, \s is a space.
  • master'?s? matches master, masters, master's.
  • m\.?\s?s\b(?=[\s.,]|$) matches M.S, and the (?=...) part is a lookahead: it demands that the next character is a space, dot, comma or the end. That stops it matching the “MS” inside “MS Office”.
  • The | character separates alternatives: match this or that.
66EDU_LABEL = {"associate": "Associate's", "bachelor": "Bachelor's", "master": "Master's", "phd": "PhD"}
Line 66

The polite spelling for each level, used when the parser builds a sentence such as Master's in Statistics.

68SECTION_HEADINGS = {
69 "skills": r"(?:technical\s+|key\s+|core\s+)?(?:skills|competencies|technologies|tech stack|skills\s*(?:&|and)\s*tools)",
70 "experience": r"(?:work\s+|professional\s+|relevant\s+)?(?:experience|employment(?:\s+history)?|work history)",
71 "education": r"education(?:al)?(?:\s+background)?|academics|qualifications",
72 "projects": r"(?:personal\s+|academic\s+|key\s+|selected\s+)?projects",
73 "summary": r"(?:professional\s+)?(?:summary|profile|objective|about(?:\s+me)?)",
74 "other": r"certifications?|achievements?|awards?|publications?|interests|hobbies|languages|references|extracurriculars?|volunteer(?:ing)?",
75}
Lines 68–75

SECTION_HEADINGS maps a section to a pattern that matches its heading line. A resume might say “Skills”, “Technical Skills” or “Core Competencies”.

  • (?:technical\s+|key\s+|core\s+)?: an optional prefix word. (?: ... ) is a group that does not capture; the ? after it means the whole group is optional.
  • skills|competencies|technologies|...: any of these words.
  • skills\s*(?:&|and)\s*tools matches “Skills & Tools” and “Skills and Tools”.
  • The education line uses education(?:al)? so “Education” and “Educational Background” both match.

These patterns match a whole line (checked later with fullmatch), so a sentence that merely mentions “projects” is not mistaken for a heading.

77MONTHS = {m: i for i, m in enumerate(
78 ["jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec"], start=1)}
Lines 77–78

A lookup from month name to number: {"jan": 1, "feb": 2, ...}. The expression is a dictionary comprehension. enumerate(list, start=1) numbers the items starting from 1, so January is 1 rather than 0.

81# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
82# Text extraction
83# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Lines 81–83

A divider comment. This section reads text out of files.

84def extract_text(data: bytes, filename: str) -> str:
85 ext = Path(filename).suffix.lower()
Lines 84–85
  • 84. extract_text receives the file's raw contents (data: bytes) and its name. Bytes are the raw ones and zeros of a file.
  • 85. Path(filename).suffix.lower() pulls out the file ending, for example .pdf.
86 if ext == ".pdf":
87 from pypdf import PdfReader
88 reader = PdfReader(io.BytesIO(data))
89 return "\n".join((page.extract_text() or "") for page in reader.pages)
Lines 86–89

If it is a PDF:

  • 87. Imports PdfReader only when needed. An import inside a branch means a user who never uploads a PDF never loads the library.
  • 88. io.BytesIO(data) wraps the raw bytes so the reader can treat them as an open file.
  • 89. Joins the text of every page with line breaks. page.extract_text() or "" uses an empty string if a page returns nothing (None).
90 if ext == ".docx":
91 import docx
92 document = docx.Document(io.BytesIO(data))
93 parts = [("- " + p.text) if p.style.name.lower().startswith("list") and p.text.strip() else p.text
94 for p in document.paragraphs]
95 for table in document.tables:
96 for row in table.rows:
97 parts.append(" ".join(cell.text for cell in row.cells))
98 return "\n".join(parts)
Lines 90–98

If it is a Word document (.docx):

  • 91 to 92. Imports the docx library and opens the document from memory.
  • 93 to 94. Makes a list with one entry per paragraph. For paragraphs whose Word style is a bullet list (style.name starting with “list”), it adds "- " in front, because Word hides the bullet symbol and we need it later to separate projects. Words like and ... else inside the brackets choose between the two cases for each paragraph.
  • 95 to 97. Resumes sometimes use tables. Each row is turned into text by joining its cell texts with two spaces, and appended to the list.
  • 98. Joins everything with line breaks.
99 if ext in (".txt", ".md", ""):
100 for enc in ("utf-8", "latin-1"):
101 try:
102 return data.decode(enc)
103 except UnicodeDecodeError:
104 continue
105 raise ValueError(f"Unsupported file type '{ext}'. Upload a PDF, DOCX or TXT resume.")
Lines 99–105

If it is a text file, or anything else:

  • 99. Plain text, markdown or no extension.
  • 100. Try two ways of decoding bytes to letters. UTF-8 handles most files; latin-1 is an older fallback.
  • 101 to 104. try: means “attempt this”. except UnicodeDecodeError: means “if that specific kind of error happens, do this instead”. continue jumps to the next encoding. If one works, return ends the function with the text.
  • 105. If the file type is not recognised, raise ValueError(...) stops with a clear message. The app catches it and shows it to the user.
108def _clean(text: str) -> str:
109 text = text.replace("•", "\n- ").replace("●", "\n- ").replace("▪", "\n- ").replace("", "\n- ")
110 text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text)
111 text = re.sub(r"\n\s*\n+", "\n\n", text)
112 return text.strip()
Lines 108–112

Tidies the extracted text. PDFs and Word files bring odd bullet symbols and spacing.

  • 109. Replaces the four common bullet symbols with a new line and a dash. After this, every bullet looks like - text. .replace(a, b) swaps one string for another; the calls are chained one after another.
  • 110. re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text): replace any run of spaces or tabs with one space.
  • 111. \n\s*\n+ finds a line break, optional spaces, and more line breaks, and replaces them with exactly one blank line.
  • 112. .strip() trims the ends. Returns the clean text.
115# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
116# Section splitting
117# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Lines 115–117

Divider comment. This section splits the text into the resume's named parts.

118def split_sections(text: str) -> dict:
119 sections = {"header": []}
120 current = "header"
121 for line in text.splitlines():
122 stripped = line.strip().rstrip(":").strip()
123 matched = None
124 if stripped and len(stripped) <= 45:
125 for name, pattern in SECTION_HEADINGS.items():
126 if re.fullmatch(pattern, stripped, flags=re.I):
127 matched = name
128 break
129 if matched:
130 current = matched
131 sections.setdefault(current, [])
132 else:
133 sections.setdefault(current, []).append(line)
134 return {k: "\n".join(v).strip() for k, v in sections.items()}
Lines 118–134

Walks down the resume line by line, tracking which section we are in.

  • 119. A dictionary of lists. Each section name maps to the lines found in it. Everything above the first heading goes to "header".
  • 120. current remembers the section we are in now.
  • 121. text.splitlines() cuts the text into lines; the loop visits each.
  • 122. Cleans the line: trim, remove a trailing colon, trim again. “Skills:” becomes “Skills”.
  • 123. matched starts as None (no heading found yet).
  • 124. Only lines of 1 to 45 characters can be headings. A long sentence cannot.
  • 125 to 128. Try each section's pattern. re.fullmatch(pattern, stripped, flags=re.I) succeeds only if the whole line fits, ignoring capital letters (re.I). On success, remember the name and break out of the loop.
  • 129 to 131. If a heading was found, switch current to it. .setdefault(current, []) creates an empty list if this section is new.
  • 132 to 133. Otherwise, the line belongs to the current section: add it.
  • 134. At the end, convert each list of lines into one text with "\n".join(v).strip().

Example: a resume with headings SKILLS, EXPERIENCE, EDUCATION gives a dictionary with keys header, skills, experience, education, each holding its own text.

137# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
138# Field extractors
139# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Lines 137–139

Divider comment. Next come the fact-finders, one for each field.

140def extract_name(text: str, filename: str = "") -> str:
141 first = True
142 for line in text.splitlines()[:8]:
143 line = line.strip()
144 if not line:
145 continue
146 if any(re.fullmatch(p, line.rstrip(":"), flags=re.I) for p in SECTION_HEADINGS.values()):
147 break # reached the first section: the name would have come before it
148 is_first, first = first, False
149 if re.search(r"[\d@/|:]", line) or len(line) > 40:
150 continue
151 words = line.split()
152 # a name is capitalised words ("and decisions." from a wrapped summary line is not), and a lone word
153 # only counts when it is the very first line of the resume
154 if (2 <= len(words) <= 4 or (is_first and len(words) == 1)) and all(
155 re.fullmatch(r"[A-Z][A-Za-z'\-]*\.?", w) and (not w.endswith(".") or len(w) == 2) for w in words
156 ):
157 return line.title() if line.isupper() else line
158 return Path(filename).stem.replace("_", " ").replace("-", " ").title() or "Unknown candidate"
Lines 140–158

Finds the candidate's name. Names are hard: they have no label. We guess that the name is a short line near the top that looks like capitalised words.

  • 141. first remembers whether we are on the very first non-empty line.
  • 142. Only the first 8 lines are checked. [:8] keeps the first eight.
  • 143 to 145. Trim the line and skip empty ones with continue.
  • 146 to 147. If this line is a section heading, stop looking. A name would appear before the first section.
  • 148. is_first, first = first, False assigns two things at once: is_first gets the old value of first, then first becomes False.
  • 149 to 150. Skip lines containing digits, @, /, | or : (contact lines), or longer than 40 characters.
  • 151. Splits the line into words.
  • 152 to 156. The test. The line must have 2 to 4 words (or exactly 1 word if it is the first line), and every word must look like a capitalised name. [A-Z][A-Za-z'\-]*\.? means a capital letter, then letters or apostrophes or hyphens, then an optional dot. A word ending in a dot must be a single initial (length 2), like “J.”.
  • 157. If all-capitals, convert with .title(); otherwise return as is.
  • 158. If no name was found, use the file name: replace underscores and hyphens with spaces and capitalise.
A real bug we fixed

A PDF wrapped a long summary so that the second line was just “and decisions.”. Two short words looked like a name, and one candidate was named “And Decisions.”. The fix is the capital-letter test on line 155 and the stop-at-first-heading rule on line 147. Real files break rules you never thought of, so keep sample files.

161def extract_email(text: str) -> str:
162 m = re.search(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", text)
163 return m.group(0) if m else ""
Lines 161–163
  • 162. Finds an email address. The pattern reads: one or more word characters, dots, plus or minus signs ([\w.+-]+), then @, then a domain, a dot, and a suffix. re.search returns the first match or None.
  • 163. m.group(0) is the matched text. The if m else "" part returns an empty string when nothing was found.
166def detect_skills(text: str, extra_terms=()) -> list:
167 """Canonical skills found in the text: built-in vocabulary plus any job-specific terms."""
168 vocab = {normalize_skill(t) for t in BUILTIN_SKILLS} | {normalize_skill(t) for t in extra_terms}
169 found = []
170 text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text) # PDFs wrap lines mid-skill ("A/B\nTesting")
171 scan = text
Lines 166–171

Finds the skills mentioned anywhere in the resume.

  • 166. extra_terms=() is an optional input, an empty tuple by default. The app passes the job's skills here, so a skill you typed (even a rare one like “golang”) is searched for.
  • 168. vocab is the set of skills to look for: the built-ins plus the extra terms, all cleaned. The | operator between two sets means union (everything from both).
  • 169. An empty list for what we find.
  • 170. Turns all whitespace, including line breaks, into single spaces. PDFs sometimes split a skill over two lines, such as A/B then Testing. Without this, the two-word skill would be missed.
  • 171. scan is a copy of the text that we will edit as we go.
172 # Multi-word skills first, masked once found, so "API testing" doesn't also count as plain "testing".
173 for canon in sorted(vocab, key=lambda c: (-len(c.split()), c)):
174 variants = [canon] + ALIAS_VARIANTS.get(canon, [])
175 hit = False
176 for v in variants:
177 if mentions(scan, v):
178 hit = True
179 if len(v.split()) > 1:
180 scan = re.sub(r"(?<![a-z0-9])" + re.escape(v) + r"(?![a-z0-9])", " ", scan, flags=re.I)
181 if hit:
182 found.append(canon)
Lines 172–182

The search loop.

  • 172. The comment explains the trick: look for multi-word skills first, and blank them out once found. Otherwise the text “API testing” would also give the separate skill “testing”.
  • 173. sorted(vocab, key=...) orders skills with the most words first. -len(c.split()) is the negative word count, so bigger counts come first.
  • 174. The skill's own name plus its safe nicknames.
  • 175 to 177. hit records whether anything matched. Try each variant with the whole-word search.
  • 178 to 180. On a match, set hit. If the variant has more than one word, re.sub replaces that phrase in scan with a space, so shorter skills cannot match inside it.
  • 181 to 182. If any variant matched, add the official skill name to found.
183 # "Spring" alone is ambiguous (the season); treat it as Spring Boot only alongside Java.
184 if "spring boot" not in found and mentions(text, "spring") and mentions(text, "java"):
185 found.append("spring boot")
186 return sorted(found)
Lines 183–186
  • 183 to 185. A special case for the word “spring”: only count Spring Boot if the resume also mentions Java. A student mentioning “Spring 2023” is not a Java developer.
  • 186. Returns the skills in alphabetical order.
189def _to_month_index(token: str, today: date):
190 token = token.strip().lower()
191 if token in ("present", "current", "now", "till date", "to date", "ongoing"):
192 return today.year * 12 + today.month
193 m = re.fullmatch(r"([a-z]{3,9})\.?,?\s*(\d{4})", token)
194 if m and m.group(1)[:3] in MONTHS:
195 return int(m.group(2)) * 12 + MONTHS[m.group(1)[:3]]
196 m = re.fullmatch(r"(\d{1,2})[/.-](\d{4})", token)
197 if m and 1 <= int(m.group(1)) <= 12:
198 return int(m.group(2)) * 12 + int(m.group(1))
199 m = re.fullmatch(r"(\d{4})", token)
200 if m and 1950 <= int(m.group(1)) <= today.year + 1:
201 return int(m.group(1)) * 12 + 1
202 return None
Lines 189–202

Converts a date such as “Jan 2019” into a single number, a month counter: year × 12 + month. With such numbers, subtracting gives months directly. January 2020 minus January 2019 is 12.

  • 190. Trim and lowercase.
  • 191 to 192. Words like “present” or “ongoing” mean now: use today's year and month.
  • 193 to 195. Matches a month name and year, like Jan 2019 or January, 2019. ([a-z]{3,9}) captures 3 to 9 letters; \d{4} is exactly four digits. m.group(1)[:3] is the first three letters of the month name, looked up in MONTHS.
  • 196 to 198. Matches a numeric month like 03/2019 and checks the month is 1 to 12.
  • 199 to 201. Matches a bare year such as 2019, treated as January of that year, if it is a believable year (1950 up to next year).
  • 202. If nothing fits, return None, meaning “not a date”.
205def years_from_date_ranges(text: str, today: date = None) -> float:
206 """Total months covered by date ranges (overlaps merged), in years."""
207 today = today or date.today()
Lines 205–207
  • 205. Takes text and an optional today, so tests can pretend it is another day.
  • 207. today = today or date.today(): if none was given, use the real date.
208 month = r"(?:jan|feb|mar|apr|may|jun|jul|aug|sep|oct|nov|dec)[a-z]*"
209 tok = rf"(?:{month}\.?,?[ \t]*\d{{4}}|\d{{1,2}}[/.-]\d{{4}}|\d{{4}}|present|current|now|ongoing|till date|to date)"
210 pattern = re.compile(rf"({tok})\s*(?:-|–|—|to|until)\s*({tok})", re.I)
Lines 208–210

Builds the pattern that finds date ranges such as Jan 2022 - Present.

  • 208. month: the first three letters of a month, then any extra letters (so “January” works).
  • 209. tok is one date token: either a month and year, a numeric month/year, a bare year, or a word like present. The rf"..." prefix means a raw f-string. Inside it, {month} is replaced by the pattern above, and {{4}} (doubled braces) is how you write a literal {4}, meaning “exactly four”.
  • 210. The full range pattern: a token, a separator (-, an en or em dash, to or until), another token. The two tokens are in parentheses so they are captured. re.compile(..., re.I) prepares the pattern for reuse and ignores capitals.
211 intervals = []
212 for a, b in pattern.findall(text):
213 start, end = _to_month_index(a, today), _to_month_index(b, today)
214 if start is None or end is None or end < start:
215 continue
216 # bare "2019 - 2021" ranges mean whole calendar years
217 if re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", b.strip()):
218 end += 11
219 intervals.append((start, end))
Lines 211–219
  • 211. The list of month intervals.
  • 212. pattern.findall(text) returns every range found, as pairs (start_text, end_text). The loop unpacks each pair into a and b.
  • 213. Convert both ends to month counters.
  • 214 to 215. Skip a range if either end is not a date or if it ends before it starts.
  • 216 to 218. If the end is a bare year (2019 - 2021), add 11 months so it means “through December”.
  • 219. Store the interval as a pair.
220 if not intervals:
221 return 0.0
222 intervals.sort()
223 merged = [list(intervals[0])]
224 for s, e in intervals[1:]:
225 if s <= merged[-1][1]:
226 merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], e)
227 else:
228 merged.append([s, e])
229 return sum(e - s for s, e in merged) / 12.0
Lines 220–229

Adds up the intervals without double-counting overlaps.

  • 220 to 221. No ranges found: 0 years.
  • 222. Sort the intervals by start date.
  • 223. merged starts with the first interval (as a list so it can be edited).
  • 224 to 228. For each next interval: if it starts before the last one ends (they overlap), stretch the last one with max(...). Otherwise add it as a new interval. Two part-time jobs held at once therefore count only once.
  • 229. Total months across all merged intervals, divided by 12 to get years.

Example: Jul 2021 - Dec 2022 and Jan 2023 - Present add up to about 5.3 years (as of October 2026).

232def years_stated(text: str) -> float:
233 best = 0.0
234 patterns = [
235 r"(\d{1,2})(?:\.\d)?\s*\+?\s*(?:years?|yrs?)\s+(?:of\s+)?(?:\w+[\s,/&-]+){0,4}?experience",
236 r"experience\s*(?:of|:)?\s*(\d{1,2})\s*\+?\s*(?:years?|yrs?)",
237 r"(\d{1,2})\s*\+?\s*(?:years?|yrs?)\s+(?:in the field|of (?:professional|industry|work))",
238 ]
Lines 232–238

Reads experience when the resume states it in words, for example “5 years of experience”.

  • 233. best keeps the largest number found.
  • 234. A list of three patterns.
  • 235. A number, years or yrs, then up to four other words, then “experience”. It covers “5+ years of professional experience”. \d{1,2} is one or two digits. \+? is an optional plus sign. {0,4}? means “zero to four, as few as possible”.
  • 236. “Experience: 5 years” order.
  • 237. “8 years in the field”.
239 for p in patterns:
240 for m in re.finditer(p, text, flags=re.I):
241 best = max(best, float(m.group(1)))
Lines 239–241

Applies each pattern. re.finditer yields each match in turn. m.group(1) is the captured number. float(...) converts text to a number and max(best, ...) keeps the larger one. So if the resume says both “2 years” and “6 years” of experience, we keep 6.

242 if best == 0.0: # looser fallback: "spent 5 years building ..."
243 for m in re.finditer(r"(\d{1,2})\s*\+?\s*(?:years?|yrs?)\b", text, flags=re.I):
244 after = text[m.end(): m.end() + 25].lower() # "4 years degree/program" is schooling, not work
245 if not re.match(r"\s*(?:of\s+)?(?:degree|bachelor|master|course|program|school|college|university)", after):
246 best = max(best, float(m.group(1)))
247 return best
Lines 242–247
  • 242. If nothing was found, use a looser fallback: any “N years”. This catches “has spent 5 years building skills”.
  • 243. Finds every number followed by years.
  • 244. text[m.end(): m.end() + 25] slices the 25 characters after the match.
  • 245 to 246. If those characters start with words like “degree” or “university”, it is schooling (“4 years degree”) and not work, so skip it. Otherwise keep the larger number.
  • 247. Returns the best figure, or 0.
A real bug we fixed

An earlier version rejected any number if a degree word appeared within 40 characters either side. That wrongly threw away “(7 years)” written next to “Master's”, and 20% of our test resumes lost their years. Looking only at the words after the number fixed it.

250def extract_education(text: str, sections: dict):
251 """Return (education_string, level_key, field) -- level/field may be None."""
252 scope = sections.get("education") or text
Lines 250–252
  • 250 to 251. Returns three things: the education sentence, the level code, and the field. The docstring warns that level or field may be None.
  • 252. scope is the text to search: the Education section if there is one, otherwise the whole resume. A or B picks A unless it is empty.
253 level = None
254 for lvl, pattern in DEGREE_PATTERNS:
255 if re.search(pattern, scope, flags=re.I):
256 level = lvl
257 break
258 if level is None and scope is not text:
259 for lvl, pattern in DEGREE_PATTERNS: # degree might sit outside the education section
260 if re.search(pattern, text, flags=re.I):
261 level, scope = lvl, text
262 break
Lines 253–262

Finds the degree level.

  • 253 to 257. Starting with no level, check each pattern from highest to lowest. The first pattern found sets the level and stops the loop.
  • 258 to 262. If nothing was found and we only searched the Education section, search the whole resume. Some resumes mention the degree in the summary. If found there, scope switches to the full text. scope is not text means “scope is a different object from the full text”.
264 field = None
265 if level:
266 degree_re = dict(DEGREE_PATTERNS)[level]
267 for line in scope.splitlines():
268 if re.search(degree_re, line, flags=re.I):
269 on_line = sorted((line.lower().find(f.lower()), -len(f), f) for f in KNOWN_FIELDS if mentions(line, f))
270 if on_line:
271 field = on_line[0][2]
272 break
Lines 264–272

Finds the field of study, preferring the one on the same line as the highest degree.

  • 265 to 266. If a level was found, dict(DEGREE_PATTERNS)[level] looks up its pattern. (A list of pairs can be turned into a dictionary with dict(...).)
  • 267 to 268. Go line by line; act only on lines that contain that degree.
  • 269. Builds a list of triples (position, -length, field) for every known field mentioned on the line. Sorting orders them by position, and when positions tie, by longer name first (the negative length). So “Computer Science” wins over “Science”.
  • 270 to 272. If any found, take the first one's field ([0][2]: first triple, third part) and stop.
A real bug we fixed

A candidate listed “M.Sc. in Statistics” and, below it, “B.Sc. in Mathematics”. The old code took the field with the longest name anywhere in the section, so the master's was reported as “Mathematics”. Matching on the degree's own line fixed it.

273 hits = [] if field else sorted((scope.lower().find(f.lower()), f) for f in KNOWN_FIELDS if mentions(scope, f))
274 if hits:
275 # keep the most specific field (e.g. "Computer Science" over "Engineering") among the earliest mentions
276 field = min(hits, key=lambda h: (h[0] // 80, -len(h[1])))[1]
277 if field is None:
278 m = re.search(r"(?:in|of)\s+([A-Z][A-Za-z&\- ]{2,40}?)(?=[,.;\n(|]|\s+(?:from|at|university|college|institute)\b)", scope)
279 if m:
280 field = m.group(1).strip()
Lines 273–280
  • 273. If no field was found on the degree's line, list all the known fields anywhere in the scope, with their positions. [] if field else sorted(...) returns an empty list when we already have a field.
  • 274 to 276. From the list, pick one. min(hits, key=lambda h: (h[0] // 80, -len(h[1]))) groups positions into zones of 80 characters (// is whole-number division) and prefers the longer name within a zone.
  • 277 to 280. A last resort for an unknown subject: capture the words after “in” or “of”, such as the “Robotics” in “B.Tech in Robotics, from MIT”. (?=...) is a lookahead that says where the phrase must end (comma, dot, bracket, or a word like “university”). m.group(1) is the captured phrase.
282 parts = [EDU_LABEL[level]] if level else []
283 if field:
284 parts.append(f"in {field}")
285 return (" ".join(parts) if parts else ""), level, field
Lines 282–285

Builds the output.

  • 282. A list holding the polite level name, such as Bachelor's, or an empty list if there is no level.
  • 283 to 284. If a field exists, add in Statistics.
  • 285. Returns three things: the joined sentence (or empty text), the level code, and the field. A single return can hand back several values.
288def extract_projects(sections: dict, limit: int = 6) -> list:
289 body = sections.get("projects", "")
290 if not body:
291 return []
292 has_markers = bool(re.search(r"^\s*(?:[-*–—]|\d+[.)])\s+", body, flags=re.M))
293 raw_entries, current = [], []
Lines 288–293

Finds the candidate's projects.

  • 289 to 291. Takes the Projects section text. If there is none, return an empty list.
  • 292. has_markers asks “do project lines start with a bullet?”. The pattern ^\s*(?:[-*–—]|\d+[.)])\s+ means: line start (^), optional spaces, a dash, star, long dash, or a number followed by a dot or bracket, then at least one space. re.M makes ^ work at the start of each line.
  • 293. Two empty lists in one line: raw_entries collects finished projects; current holds the one being read.
294 for line in body.splitlines():
295 if not has_markers and line.strip() and re.match(r"^[A-Z][^:\n]{2,60}(?::|\s[–—-]\s)", line.strip()):
296 if current:
297 raw_entries.append(" ".join(current))
298 current = [line.strip()]
Lines 294–298
  • 294. Visit each line of the section.
  • 295 to 298. For resumes without bullets: a line that starts with a capital and has a Title: or Title - shape begins a new project. Save the previous one and start a fresh current.
299 elif re.match(r"^\s*(?:[-*–—]|\d+[.)])\s+", line) or (not line.strip() and current):
300 if current:
301 raw_entries.append(" ".join(current))
302 current = [] if not line.strip() else [re.sub(r"^\s*(?:[-*–—]|\d+[.)])\s+", "", line).strip()]
303 elif line.strip():
304 current.append(line.strip())
Lines 299–304
  • 299. A bullet line, or a blank line after something has been read, marks a boundary.
  • 300 to 301. Save the project read so far.
  • 302. Start a new one. If the line was a bullet, strip the bullet marker with re.sub. If it was only a blank, start empty.
  • 303 to 304. Any other non-empty line continues the current project. This is how a description that wraps onto two lines is kept whole.
305 if current:
306 raw_entries.append(" ".join(current))
Lines 305–306

After the loop, save the last project, which would otherwise be lost because no new bullet comes after it.

308 projects = []
309 for entry in raw_entries[:limit]:
310 m = re.match(r"^(.{3,70}?)\s*(?::|\s[–—-]\s|\|)\s*(.+)$", entry)
311 title, desc = (m.group(1), m.group(2)) if m else (entry[:60], entry)
312 projects.append({"title": title.strip(), "description": desc.strip()})
313 return projects
Lines 308–313

Splits each project into a title and a description.

  • 308. The list of finished projects.
  • 309. Take at most limit (6) entries. [:limit] is the same slicing as before.
  • 310. The pattern: capture a title of 3 to 70 characters (as short as possible, because of the ?), then a separator (a colon, a dash with spaces around it, or a pipe), then capture the rest as the description.
  • 311. If it matched, title and description come from the two captured groups. If not, use the first 60 characters as the title and the whole entry as the description.
  • 312. Adds a dictionary with both parts.
  • 313. Returns the list.

319def parse_resume(text: str, filename: str = "resume.txt", extra_terms=(), today: date = None) -> dict:
320 """Parse resume text into the record format used by feature_engineering.compute_features."""
321 warnings = []
322 text = _clean(text)
323 if len(text) < 150:
324 warnings.append("Very little text was extracted. The file may be a scanned image (OCR is not supported).")
Lines 319–324

parse_resume is the one function the rest of the project calls.

  • 319. Inputs: the text, the file name, optional extra skills to hunt for, and an optional date. The last two have defaults.
  • 321. An empty list that collects warnings.
  • 322. Cleans the text.
  • 323 to 324. If the text is under 150 characters, warn that the file may be a scanned image. A scanned page has no real text and we do not do OCR (reading pictures of letters).
326 sections = split_sections(text)
327 skills = detect_skills(text, extra_terms)
328 if not skills:
329 warnings.append("No recognizable skills were detected.")
Lines 326–329
  • 326. Splits into sections.
  • 327. Finds skills, passing the job's own skills as extra terms.
  • 328 to 329. If none were found, add a warning.
331 exp_scope = sections.get("experience")
332 if exp_scope is None:
333 exp_scope = text.replace(sections.get("education", "\0"), "") # keep education dates out
334 from_dates = years_from_date_ranges(exp_scope, today)
335 stated = years_stated(text)
336 years = max(from_dates, stated)
337 if years == 0:
338 warnings.append("Could not determine years of experience; assuming 0.")
339 method = "date ranges" if from_dates >= stated and from_dates > 0 else ("stated in text" if stated else "unknown")
Lines 331–339

Works out years of experience from two sources and trusts the larger.

  • 331. The Experience section, if the resume has one.
  • 332 to 333. If not, use the whole resume with the Education text removed (.replace(education_text, "")), so degree dates such as “2018 – 2021” are not counted as work. "\0" is a harmless placeholder that never matches.
  • 334. Years from date ranges.
  • 335. Years stated in words.
  • 336. max(...) takes the larger of the two.
  • 337 to 338. If both gave zero, warn the user, and we assume 0.
  • 339. Records how we got the number, for transparency. This chained conditional reads: if dates gave at least as much and more than zero, say “date ranges”; otherwise if a stated number exists, say “stated in text”; otherwise “unknown”.
341 education, level, field = extract_education(text, sections)
342 if level is None:
343 warnings.append("No degree detected; education is scored as a bachelor's-equivalent default.")
344 education = education or "Bachelor's (assumed)"
345 if field is None:
346 warnings.append("Field of study not detected; only degree level is compared.")
Lines 341–346
  • 341. Calls the education finder, unpacking its three results.
  • 342 to 344. If no degree was found, warn, and use the stand-in Bachelor's (assumed). The feature code reads this as a bachelor's, a neutral middle assumption.
  • 345 to 346. If no field was found, warn that only the degree level will be compared.
348 projects = extract_projects(sections)
349 if not projects:
350 warnings.append("No 'Projects' section found; project relevance scores 0 for this resume.")
Lines 348–350
  • 348. Finds projects.
  • 349 to 350. If there are none, warn that project relevance will be 0 for this resume. This is honest: a resume without a Projects section is penalised on that feature, and the warning tells the user why.
352 return {
353 "name": extract_name(text, filename),
354 "email": extract_email(text),
355 "skills": skills,
356 "technologies": list(skills), # a free-form resume doesn't separate "skills" from "tools"
357 "experience_years": round(years, 1),
358 "experience_method": method,
359 "education": education,
360 "education_level": level,
361 "education_field": field,
362 "projects": projects,
363 "resume_text": text,
364 "warnings": warnings,
365 }
Lines 352–365

Returns the finished record, with the same keys the model's feature code expects:

  • 353 to 354. Name and email.
  • 355 to 356. skills and technologies. A free-form resume does not separate “skills” from “tools”, so both get the same list. list(skills) makes a separate copy.
  • 357 to 358. Years (rounded to one decimal) and which method produced them.
  • 359 to 361. The education sentence, level and field.
  • 362 to 363. The projects, and the full cleaned text (used for the similarity feature).
  • 364. The list of warnings.
Remember
  • Parsing means pulling facts out of messy text.
  • Rule-based parsing uses word lists and patterns. It is predictable, but it can fail on unusual layouts, so it reports warnings.
  • Many of the bugs here were found only by feeding in real-looking files. Keep realistic samples and re-test after every change.
  • Our test: parsing the text of 600 synthetic resumes recovered 98.6% of skills, and the years and degree level were right every time.
Honest limit

This parser cannot read scanned images, handles two-column layouts poorly, and knows only the skills in its list plus the ones you type as requirements. It is a good teaching parser and a reasonable first filter. It is not a replacement for a person reading the resume.

Try it 
cd src
python -c "import resume_parser as rp; t = rp.extract_text(open('../sample_resumes/Rishab.docx','rb').read(), 'Rishab.docx'); p = rp.parse_resume(t, 'Rishab.docx'); print(p['name'], p['experience_years'], p['education'], p['skills'])"

Then open sample_resumes/Rishab.docx in Word and compare. Try deleting the “Projects” heading, save a copy, parse it, and read the warning.

Chapter 13 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 185 lines

matcher.py

The engine room. Give it a job and a pile of applicants and it returns a ranked table with a score, skill gaps and an explanation for each one.

Up to now we trained a model on fixed data. A useful tool must work on new input: a job you type today and resumes you upload today. matcher.py is the part that does that. It reuses the same feature code and the same trained model as training, so a new candidate is measured exactly as the training candidates were.

Analogy

Training was like teaching a judge how to score a gymnastics routine. This file is the competition day: gymnasts arrive, the judge scores each routine, and a scoreboard sorts them. The judge (the trained model) is not retrained. He is just used.

Requirementsmake_job+Applicantsprepare_candidates→7 features eachcompute_features→Model probabilitypredict_proba→SHAP reasonsexplainer→Sorted tablescore_candidates

This file introduces one new idea: a class. A class is a blueprint for a bundle of related data. We use one to hold everything loaded from disk, so it is loaded only once.

  • 59. The docstring shows an example of input and output.
  • 60. A comprehension with two for parts. text.replace(";", ",") treats semicolons like commas. .splitlines() cuts at line breaks. For each line, chunk.split(",") cuts at commas. Each piece is trimmed and lowercased. Read it as: “for each line, for each piece in that line, tidy it”.
  • 61. Two things in one line: seen, an empty set, and out, an empty list.
  • 62 to 65. Go through the pieces. Skip empty ones. Skip a piece if its official form was already seen, so typing both ML and machine learning keeps only the first. Otherwise remember it and add it to the result, keeping the original order.
  • 66. Returns the list.
69def build_description(job: dict) -> str:
70 """Job-description text written in the same register as the training descriptions."""
71 req = ", ".join(job["required_skills"])
72 pref = ", ".join(job["preferred_skills"])
73 tech = ", ".join(job["technologies"])
74 text = (
75 f"We are seeking a {job['title']} to join our team. The ideal candidate will have strong experience in {req}. "
76 )
77 if pref:
78 text += f"Experience with {pref} is a plus. "
79 text += (
80 f"Requires a minimum of {job['min_experience']} years of relevant experience and a "
81 f"{job['education']}. "
82 )
83 if tech:
84 text += f"Our stack is built on {tech}."
85 return text

The model's similarity feature compares the resume text with the job's text. If the user did not paste a job description, we write one from the form, in the same style as the training descriptions.

  • 71 to 73. ", ".join(list) turns each list into text like python, sql, pandas.
  • 74 to 76. Starts the description with an f-string. The parentheses just allow the long line to be written across lines.
  • 77 to 78. if pref: adds the preferred-skills sentence only when there are any. text += appends to the end of the existing text.
  • 79 to 82. Adds the experience and education sentence.
  • 83 to 84. Adds the tools sentence if there are tools.

92 "id": "CUSTOM",
93 "title": title.strip() or "Open role",
94 "required_skills": required,
95 "preferred_skills": preferred,

The job dictionary:

111def _skill_gaps(candidate_skills, job_skills):
112 cand = normalize_skills(candidate_skills)
113 matched = [s for s in job_skills if normalize_skill(s) in cand]
114 missing = [s for s in job_skills if normalize_skill(s) not in cand]
115 return matched, missing
Lines 111–115

Works out which of the job's skills a candidate has and which they lack.

  • 112. The candidate's cleaned skills as a set.
  • 113. matched: for each job skill, keep it if its cleaned form is in the candidate's set. We keep the job's own wording so the app shows what the recruiter typed.
  • 114. missing: the same list with the test reversed (not in).
  • 115. Returns both lists.
118def prepare_candidates(job: dict, pool: list, uploads: list) -> list:
119 """
120 pool : structured resume dicts (bundled dataset)
121 uploads : [{"filename": str, "text": str}] raw text from uploaded files
122 Uploads are parsed per job so any skill typed into the requirements is detected, not just a fixed list.
123 """
Lines 118–123

Gathers everyone to be scored. The docstring explains the two sources: the structured pool and raw-text uploads. Uploads are parsed for each job, so any skill you type is searched for, even a rare one.

124 extra = job["required_skills"] + job["preferred_skills"] + job["technologies"]
125 candidates = []
126 for r in pool:
127 candidates.append({**r, "source": "Pool", "key": r["id"], "email": "", "warnings": []})
128 for up in uploads:
129 parsed = parse_resume(up["text"], up["filename"], extra_terms=extra)
130 parsed.update({"source": "Uploaded", "key": f"U:{up['filename']}", "id": f"U:{up['filename']}"})
131 candidates.append(parsed)
132 return candidates
Lines 124–132
  • 124. extra: all of the job's skills and tools, joined. Passed to the parser as extra terms to hunt for.
  • 125. An empty list for the candidates.
  • 126 to 127. For each pool resume, append a copy with extra labels. {**r, "source": "Pool", ...} means “copy everything in r and add these keys”. The pool has no email and no warnings, so those are set to empty.
  • 128 to 131. For each upload: parse its text, then parsed.update({...}) adds more keys: source (“Uploaded”), a unique key, and an id built from the file name, such as U:Rishab.docx. Then append.
  • 132. Returns the list.
135def score_candidates(art: Artifacts, job: dict, candidates: list) -> pd.DataFrame:
136 """One row per candidate with features, probability, SHAP contributions and skill gaps."""
137 if not candidates:
138 return pd.DataFrame()
Lines 135–138
  • 135. score_candidates takes the loaded artifacts, a job and the candidates. It returns a table. The : Artifacts and -> pd.DataFrame are hints for readers.
  • 137 to 138. Guard: with no candidates, return an empty table.
140 job_vec = art.vectorizer.transform([job["description_text"]])
141 resume_vecs = art.vectorizer.transform([c["resume_text"] for c in candidates])
142 sims = cosine_similarity(resume_vecs, job_vec).ravel()
Lines 140–142

The similarity feature.

  • 140. art.vectorizer.transform([...]) turns the job's text into numbers. This uses transform, not fit: it applies the vocabulary learned during training and does not learn a new one.
  • 141. The same for every candidate's resume text.
  • 142. cosine_similarity(resume_vecs, job_vec) compares all resumes against the job at once and gives a column of numbers. .ravel() flattens it into a simple one-dimensional list.
144 feats = pd.DataFrame(
145 [compute_features(c, job, float(sim)) for c, sim in zip(candidates, sims)]
146 )[FEATURES]
Lines 144–146
  • 144 to 146. For each candidate and its similarity (zip pairs them), call compute_features. The list of dictionaries becomes a table, and [FEATURES] reorders its columns into the training order. This is the table the model scores.
147 proba = art.model.predict_proba(feats)[:, 1]
148 shap_values = art.explainer(feats).values
Lines 147–148
  • 147. predict_proba(feats)[:, 1]: every candidate's probability of being a good match. [:, 1] means “all rows, second column”.
  • 148. SHAP contributions for everyone at once. .values is the table of numbers (candidates by features).
150 rows = []
151 for i, c in enumerate(candidates):
152 req_matched, req_missing = _skill_gaps(c["skills"], job["required_skills"])
153 pref_matched, pref_missing = _skill_gaps(c["skills"], job["preferred_skills"])
154 contribs = dict(zip(FEATURES, shap_values[i].tolist()))
155 pos = [f for f, v in sorted(contribs.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]) if v > 0]
156 neg = [f for f, v in sorted(contribs.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) if v < 0]
Lines 150–156

Now build one results row per candidate.

  • 150. The list of rows.
  • 151. enumerate(candidates) gives each candidate with its position i.
  • 152 to 153. Skill gaps for required and preferred skills.
  • 154. The SHAP numbers for this candidate as a dictionary, feature name to number. .tolist() converts to plain numbers.
  • 155. pos: feature names with a positive push, ordered biggest first. -kv[1] sorts descending, because the minus sign flips the order.
  • 156. neg: negative pushes, most negative first.
157 rows.append({
158 "key": c["key"],
159 "name": c["name"],
160 "source": c["source"],
161 "email": c.get("email", ""),
162 "score": float(proba[i]),
163 "verdict": "Good match" if proba[i] >= 0.5 else "Poor match",
164 "experience_years": c["experience_years"],
165 "education": c["education"],
166 "required_matched": req_matched,
167 "required_missing": req_missing,
168 "preferred_matched": pref_matched,
169 "preferred_missing": pref_missing,
170 "contributions": contribs,
171 "narrative": narrative(c["name"], job["title"], float(proba[i]), pos, neg),
172 "warnings": c.get("warnings", []),
173 "projects": c.get("projects", []),
174 "skills": c["skills"],
175 **{f: float(feats.iloc[i][f]) for f in FEATURES},
176 })
Lines 157–176

One row of the final table, as a dictionary:

  • 158 to 161. Identity: a key, the name, where the resume came from, an email if any. c.get("email", "") avoids an error if the key is missing.
  • 162 to 163. The score (probability) and the verdict, using the 0.5 cut-off.
  • 164 to 165. Years of experience and education, shown in the table.
  • 166 to 169. The four skill lists: required matched and missing, preferred matched and missing.
  • 170. The SHAP contributions, for the chart.
  • 171. The plain-English sentence from narrative.
  • 172 to 174. Parser warnings, projects and skills.
  • 175. **{...} spreads the seven feature values into the row as seven more columns, so the whole ranking can be downloaded.
177 df = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
178 df.insert(0, "rank", df.index + 1)
179 return df
Lines 177–179
  • 177. Builds the table from the rows. sort_values("score", ascending=False) puts the highest score first. reset_index(drop=True) renumbers the rows 0, 1, 2...
  • 178. Inserts a rank column at the front: row number plus 1, so the best candidate is rank 1.
  • 179. Returns the finished ranking.
182__all__ = [
183 "Artifacts", "FEATURES", "FEATURE_LABELS", "NEGATIVE_PHRASES", "POSITIVE_PHRASES",
184 "make_job", "split_terms", "prepare_candidates", "score_candidates", "EDU_LABEL",
185]
Lines 182–185

__all__ lists the names this file offers to others. The app uses m.FEATURES, m.make_job, m.score_candidates and so on, where m is this module.

Remember
  • Training and use share the same feature code and the same model, which is why a new resume is measured fairly.
  • A class is a bundle of related data. self means “this object”.
  • TF-IDF is fitted once during training, then only transformed afterwards.
  • Scoring 605 candidates, including SHAP, takes about 0.3 seconds.
Try it 
cd src
python -c "import matcher as m; a = m.Artifacts(); job = m.make_job('Data Analyst', ['sql','python','excel'], ['tableau'], [], 2, 'bachelor'); df = m.score_candidates(a, job, m.prepare_candidates(job, a.pool, [])); print(df[['rank','name','score']].head())"

That prints the five best bundled candidates for a Data Analyst role.

Chapter 14 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 295 lines

app.py

The face of the project. A web page, written entirely in Python, where you type a job, add resumes and see a ranked list with explanations.

Everything so far ran in a terminal and printed text. Most people want buttons and tables. Streamlit is a library that turns a Python script into a web page, without writing any HTML or JavaScript. Each line that says st.something(...) puts something on the page: a title, a text box, a chart.

The one idea that explains this whole file

Streamlit re-runs the entire script from the top, every time the user does anything: click, type, move a slider. There is no “when the button is clicked, call this function”. Instead, widgets return their current value each time the script runs, and your code reacts to those values.

Analogy

Imagine a waiter who, whenever you change anything on your order, reads the whole order again from line one. Simple to reason about, but wasteful if reading takes long. So Streamlit gives you two tools: caching (“do this slow thing once and remember the answer”) and session state (“a notebook that survives the re-reads”). You will see both below.

The file has five regions: setup (imports and constants), helper functions, the sidebar (where you describe the job), the scoring step (when you press the button), and three tabs (Ranking, Model insights, How it works).

44def shap_chart(contributions: dict):
45 items = sorted(contributions.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
46 labels = [m.FEATURE_LABELS[k] for k, _ in items]
47 values = [v for _, v in items]
48 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.4))
49 ax.barh(labels, values, color=[GREEN if v > 0 else RED for v in values])
50 ax.axvline(0, color="#888", linewidth=0.8)
51 ax.set_xlabel("Contribution to match score (SHAP, log-odds)")
52 for spine in ("top", "right"):
53 ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
54 fig.tight_layout()
55 return fig
Lines 44–55

Draws the “Why this score” chart for one candidate.

  • 45. Sorts the (feature, number) pairs from smallest to largest.
  • 46 to 47. Two lists: the friendly labels, and the numbers.
  • 48. plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.4)) creates a blank chart. It returns two things: the whole picture (fig) and the drawing area (ax). figsize is width and height in inches.
  • 49. ax.barh(...) draws horizontal bars. The color=[...] list gives each bar green if its value is positive, red otherwise.
  • 50. ax.axvline(0, ...) draws a vertical grey line at zero, the dividing line between pushing up and pushing down.
  • 51. The label under the chart.
  • 52 to 53. Hides the top and right border lines for a cleaner look.
  • 54 to 55. Fixes the spacing and returns the picture.

275with tab_how:
276 st.markdown(
277 """
278**Pipeline** (slide 4): resume + job description → text extraction → information extraction → skill
279normalization → feature engineering → Logistic Regression → match probability → SHAP explanation.
280
281**The 7 features** (slide 5), each computed for every applicant against *your* requirements:
282required-skill match, preferred-skill match, experience vs. requirement, education (degree level and field),
283technology overlap, project relevance, and TF-IDF semantic similarity between the resume and the job text.
284
285**Resume parsing** is rule-based: it reads PDF/DOCX/TXT, splits sections (Skills, Experience, Education,
286Projects), finds skills from a vocabulary plus anything you typed as a requirement (aliases like *k8s*, *ML*
287are normalized), sums date ranges for years of experience, and detects degree level and field. Anything it could
288not find is flagged under the candidate. Scanned/image-only PDFs are not supported (no OCR).
289
290**Limitations**
291- Trained on synthetic data with simulated recruiter labels; treat scores as decision support, not decisions.
292- The model is linear, so experience is a weighted factor, not a hard cut-off. Use the filter above if it is one.
293- SHAP explains the *model's* behaviour; it does not prove the prediction is correct or fair.
294 """
295 )
Lines 275–295

The How it works tab is one long piece of text in Markdown, a simple way to format text. Between the triple quotes, **word** makes bold, *word* makes italic and a line starting with - makes a bullet. The text summarises the pipeline, the seven features, how parsing works and the limitations, for anyone using the app.

Remember
  • Streamlit re-runs the whole script on every interaction. That one fact explains the structure.
  • Caching (cache_resource) avoids repeating slow work. Session state keeps results between re-runs.
  • A form batches inputs until the button is pressed.
  • The app contains almost no logic of its own. It collects input, calls matcher.py, and displays the answer.
Try it 
streamlit run app.py

Pick the Data Analyst setup from chapter 16, or the Data Scientist template. Press Find best applicants. Click different rows and watch the explanation change. Tick the hard experience filter and see who disappears.

Chapter 15 · Part III · The code, in the order it runs · 252 lines

generate_dataset.py

The optional route. Instead of building resumes from templates, it asks an AI model (Claude) over the internet to write the job descriptions and resumes.

This was the project's original way to get data. We did not end up using it for the final dataset, because it needs an API key (a password for a paid service) and costs money for every request. The offline file in chapter 7 does the job for free. It is explained here because it is part of the project, and because it teaches how a program talks to an AI service.

Analogy

An API is a restaurant's order window. You do not enter the kitchen. You hand over a written order (the prompt), pay with your account (the API key), and receive a finished dish (the AI's text). This file writes 10 orders for job descriptions and 200 orders for resumes.

The resumes it creates have no recruiter label, since no simulation runs here. When feature_engineering.py meets such resumes, it uses its fallback labelling (chapter 8, lines 149 to 154). That is the reason the fallback exists.

To use this route you would set the key and run python src/generate_dataset.py --num-pairs 200. Nothing else in the project needs it.

2Generate a synthetic resume-job dataset using the Anthropic Claude API.

4Addresses the "synthetic training data" limitation noted in the project
5(slide 8) by producing realistic, structured resumes against a fixed set of
6job postings, with controlled match quality so the resulting dataset has a
7meaningful spread of good/poor matches for the downstream Logistic

110def _extract_json(text: str) -> dict:
111 text = text.strip()
112 match = re.search(r"\{.*\}", text, re.DOTALL)
113 if not match:
114 raise ValueError(f"No JSON object found in response: {text[:200]}")
115 return json.loads(match.group(0))
Lines 110–115

AI replies are text. We asked for JSON, but the model may add polite words around it. This function digs the JSON out.

  • 111. Trim spaces.
  • 112. re.search(r"\{.*\}", text, re.DOTALL) looks for an opening curly bracket, anything at all, then a closing one. re.DOTALL makes “anything” include line breaks. So it grabs everything from the first { to the last }.
  • 113 to 114. If nothing was found, raise ValueError(...) stops with a message that includes the first 200 characters of the reply (text[:200]) so you can see what went wrong.
  • 115. match.group(0) is the matched text, and json.loads(...) converts that text into a Python dictionary.
118def generate_job_description(job: dict) -> str:
119 prompt = f"""Write a realistic, concise job description (120-180 words) for the role
120"{job['title']}". It must mention these required skills: {', '.join(job['required_skills'])}.
121It should also mention these preferred/nice-to-have skills: {', '.join(job['preferred_skills'])}.
122State the minimum experience as {job['min_experience']}+ years and the education requirement:
123"{job['education']}". Return plain text only, no markdown, no headers."""
Lines 118–123

Writes a job description by asking the AI.

  • 118. The function takes one job.
  • 119 to 123. The prompt: a long f-string inside triple quotes (so it can span lines). The curly brackets are filled in: the job title, the lists of skills joined with commas, the years and the education. The prompt sets the rules: 120 to 180 words, plain text, no formatting. A prompt is simply careful instructions.
124 resp = CLIENT.messages.create(
125 model=MODEL, max_tokens=400,
126 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
127 )
128 return resp.content[0].text.strip()
Lines 124–128
  • 124 to 127. CLIENT.messages.create(...) sends the request. model chooses the AI. max_tokens=400 caps the reply length (a token is roughly three quarters of a word). messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}] is the conversation: one message from the user.
  • 128. The reply holds a list of pieces; resp.content[0].text is the text of the first. .strip() trims it, and return hands it back.

133 "This candidate should be a STRONG match: they should possess 80-100% of the "
134 "required skills, meet or exceed the minimum experience, hold the required "
135 "education level, list most of the job's technologies, and have 2-3 projects "
136 "clearly relevant to this role."
137 ),
138 "medium": (
139 "This candidate should be a MEDIUM match: they should possess roughly 40-65% of "
140 "the required skills, have experience close to but somewhat below the minimum "
141 "(e.g. 1 year short), have a related but not exact education background, overlap "
142 "with only some of the job's technologies, and have 1-2 projects of partial relevance."
143 ),
144 "weak": (
145 "This candidate should be a WEAK match: they should possess fewer than 30% of the "
146 "required skills, have noticeably less experience than the minimum requirement, "
147 "an unrelated education background, little to no overlap with the job's "
148 "technologies, and projects unrelated to this role."
149 ),
150}
Lines 131–150

TIER_INSTRUCTIONS maps each quality level to a paragraph of instructions for the AI. For strong: have 80 to 100% of the required skills, meet the experience, list most technologies, and have two or three relevant projects. For weak: fewer than 30% of the skills, much less experience, unrelated education and projects. These are the same ideas as the hidden quality q in chapter 7, but spoken in words to an AI. The quoted pieces inside brackets are glued into one string.

153def generate_resume(job: dict, tier: str, idx: int) -> dict:
154 prompt = f"""You are generating a SYNTHETIC resume for a machine learning training dataset.
155Target job: "{job['title']}".
156Job required skills: {', '.join(job['required_skills'])}.
157Job preferred skills: {', '.join(job['preferred_skills'])}.
158Job technologies: {', '.join(job['technologies'])}.
159Job minimum experience: {job['min_experience']} years.
160Job education requirement: {job['education']}.
161
162{TIER_INSTRUCTIONS[tier]}
Lines 153–162

Writes one resume by asking the AI.

  • 153. Receives a job, a quality level and a number (idx).
  • 154 to 160. The prompt begins by telling the AI it is making synthetic data for a training set, then lists the target job's details with f-string blanks.
  • 162. {TIER_INSTRUCTIONS[tier]} inserts the right paragraph for the chosen quality level.
164Return ONLY a JSON object with this exact shape (no markdown fences, no commentary):
165{{
166 "name": "<realistic fake full name>",
167 "skills": ["<skill1>", "<skill2>", ...],
168 "experience_years": <number>,
169 "education": "<degree and field, e.g. Bachelor's in Computer Science>",
170 "technologies": ["<tech1>", "<tech2>", ...],
171 "projects": [{{"title": "<project title>", "description": "<1 sentence description>"}}, ...],
172 "resume_text": "<a realistic 150-220 word resume summary paragraph combining the above>"
173}}
174Lowercase all entries in "skills" and "technologies" for consistency."""
Lines 164–174
  • 164 to 173. The prompt demands the reply in an exact JSON shape: name, skills, years, education, technologies, projects and a text summary. Notice the double curly brackets {{ and }}. In an f-string, single braces mean “fill in a value”, so doubling them is how you write a real brace.
  • 174. Asks for lowercase skills so the later comparison is consistent.
175 resp = CLIENT.messages.create(
176 model=MODEL, max_tokens=900,
177 messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
178 )
179 data = _extract_json(resp.content[0].text)
180 data["id"] = f"R{idx:04d}"
181 data["job_id"] = job["id"]
182 data["tier"] = tier
183 return data
Lines 175–183
  • 175 to 178. Sends the request, allowing up to 900 tokens, since a resume is longer than a job description.
  • 179. Digs the JSON out of the reply and turns it into a dictionary.
  • 180 to 182. Adds three keys: an id like R0007 (:04d pads to four digits), the job id, and the tier.
  • 183. Returns the resume.
186def pick_tier() -> str:
187 r = random.random()
188 cum = 0.0
189 for tier, weight in TIERS:
190 cum += weight
191 if r <= cum:
192 return tier
193 return TIERS[-1][0]
Lines 186–193

Picks a quality level with the chances in TIERS.

  • 187. random.random() gives a number from 0 to 1.
  • 188. cum is a running total, starting at 0.
  • 189 to 192. Go through the tiers adding each chance to the total. The first time the random number is at or below the total, return that tier. With 0.4, 0.35 and 0.25 the totals are 0.4, 0.75 and 1.0. A random number of 0.6 falls at or below 0.75, so it picks the second tier, “medium”.
  • 193. A safety net: if rounding errors leave no match, return the last tier. TIERS[-1][0] means the last pair's first item.
196def main():
197 parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
198 parser.add_argument("--num-pairs", type=int, default=200)
199 parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=42)
200 parser.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=8)
201 args = parser.parse_args()
Lines 196–201

main() reads three options: how many resumes (200), the random seed (42), and the number of workers (8), the count of requests sent at the same time.

203 if not os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"):
204 raise SystemExit(
205 "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set. Set it in your environment before running:\n"
206 " setx ANTHROPIC_API_KEY \"sk-ant-...\" (Windows, new shells)\n"

208 )
Lines 203–208

A friendly check. os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") returns nothing if the key is not set. If so, raise SystemExit(...) stops and prints instructions for Windows: setx saves the key for future windows, and $env:... sets it for the current PowerShell window. The backslashes before the quotation marks let a quote appear inside the message.

210 random.seed(args.seed)
211 DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Lines 210–211
  • 210. Makes the randomness repeatable with the seed.
  • 211. Makes sure the data folder exists.
213 print(f"Generating {len(JOB_TEMPLATES)} job descriptions...")
214 jobs = []
215 with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.workers) as pool:
216 futures = {pool.submit(generate_job_description, job): job for job in JOB_TEMPLATES}
217 for fut in tqdm(as_completed(futures), total=len(futures)):
218 job = futures[fut]
219 job_out = dict(job)
220 job_out["description_text"] = fut.result()
221 jobs.append(job_out)
222 jobs.sort(key=lambda j: j["id"])
223 with open(DATA_DIR / "jobs.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
224 json.dump(jobs, f, indent=2)
Lines 213–224

Writes all 10 job descriptions at once.

  • 213 to 214. Prints a message and starts an empty list.
  • 215. ThreadPoolExecutor is a team of workers that run tasks in parallel. Each request spends most of its time waiting for the internet, so while one waits, another can start. Eight at a time is much faster than one after another.
  • 216. pool.submit(function, argument) gives a task to the team and returns a future, a promise of a result later. The dictionary comprehension stores each future together with its job.
  • 217. as_completed(...) hands back futures as they finish, in whatever order. tqdm(..., total=...) shows the progress bar.
  • 218 to 221. For each finished one: find its job, make a copy with dict(job), add the AI's text from fut.result() (which is the returned description), and add it to the list.
  • 222. Sorts by id. key=lambda j: j["id"] says “sort by the id”.
  • 223 to 224. Saves jobs.json.
226 jobs_by_id = {j["id"]: j for j in jobs}
227 assignments = [
228 (random.choice(JOB_TEMPLATES), pick_tier(), i)
229 for i in range(args.num_pairs)
230 ]
Lines 226–230
  • 226. A lookup from job id to the finished job, so resumes can use the descriptions.
  • 227 to 230. Decides in advance what every resume will be: a random job, a random quality level and a number, for each of the 200. A list of three-part tuples.
232 print(f"Generating {args.num_pairs} synthetic resumes...")
233 resumes = []
234 with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=args.workers) as pool:
235 futures = {
236 pool.submit(generate_resume, jobs_by_id[job["id"]], tier, idx): idx
237 for job, tier, idx in assignments
238 }
239 for fut in tqdm(as_completed(futures), total=len(futures)):
240 try:
241 resumes.append(fut.result())
242 except Exception as e:
243 print(f" skipped one resume due to error: {e}")
244 resumes.sort(key=lambda r: r["id"])
245 with open(DATA_DIR / "resumes.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
246 json.dump(resumes, f, indent=2)
Lines 232–246

Writes all the resumes in parallel, the same way.

  • 232 to 234. Message, empty list, and the team of workers.
  • 235 to 238. Gives each resume task to the team.
  • 239. Collects results as they finish.
  • 240 to 243. try: adds the finished resume. except Exception as e: catches any failure, such as a bad reply, prints a short note, and moves on. One bad resume does not stop the other 199.
  • 244. Sorts by id.
  • 245 to 246. Saves resumes.json.
248 print(f"Done. Wrote {len(jobs)} jobs and {len(resumes)} resumes to {DATA_DIR}")
Line 248

Prints how many jobs and resumes were written.

251if __name__ == "__main__":
252 main()
Lines 251–252

The standard guard: run main() only when the file is started directly.

Remember
  • An API lets your program use someone else's service. A prompt is the written instruction you send.
  • Many slow requests can run at once with a thread pool.
  • AI replies can be messy, so extract the part you need and expect some failures.
  • This route needs a paid key. The offline route in chapter 7 does the same job for free.
Why we did not use it

It makes the resumes look realistic, but it gives no recruiter labels, is not repeatable (the AI can answer differently each time), and costs money. The offline version fixes all three problems.

Chapter 16 · Part IV · Wrap-up

What we built, found and fixed

The numbers

These come straight from outputs/metrics.json, produced by train_model.py.

MeasureExam set (150 rows)5-fold average
Accuracy0.9070.932 ± 0.013
Precision0.875–
Recall0.875–
F10.8750.908
ROC-AUC0.9560.968

In words: the model is right about nine times in ten, and its ranking of good above poor is excellent. The five repeats agree closely, so the result is stable. All of this is measured against a simulated recruiter (chapter 2), so it shows the model learned that recruiter's tastes. It says nothing about real hiring.

What the model learned

Each weight says how strongly a feature pulls the score. The “average” column is the typical value across the 600 rows.

Featureweightaverage value
required_skill_match4.480.38
preferred_skill_match1.240.33
experience_match0.680.99
education_match0.810.83
technology_match1.120.36
project_relevance2.060.39
semantic_similarity0.600.17

Required skills dominate (4.48), then projects (2.06). Education, technologies and preferred skills are moderate. Experience (0.68) and text similarity (0.60) matter least. This agrees with how the simulated recruiter in author_dataset.py weighted things, with one difference worth noticing. The recruiter scores experience on an S-curve (a couple of years short hurts a lot), and a single straight weight cannot copy a curve. That is why the model underrates experience, and it is a real, visible limit of a linear model.

The audit: what was wrong with version 1

The first dataset looked fine and the model ran. It was only when we checked the data itself that problems appeared. This is an important habit: a model that runs is not a model that is right.

Problem foundEvidenceThe fixSee
Too little data100 rows gave a 25-row exam. Cross-validation scores ranged from 0.75 to 1.00.600 rows, a 150-row exam, 5-fold cross-validation.7, 9
Features gave away the tierproject_relevance was exactly 0, 0.5 or 1 depending on the tier. Required-skill share had two values per tier.A hidden continuous quality q per resume, with random skill sampling and extra irrelevant skills.7
Skill normalization could not be testedEvery skill was already spelled the official way.Resumes now use nicknames and capitals (“k8s”, “Html”).6, 7
Education ignored the subjectA Fine Arts bachelor's scored the same as a Computer Science one.Degree level times a field-of-study multiplier.8
A substring bug“java” matched inside “javascript” when judging projects.Whole-word matching.6
Circular labelsThe label was the same seven features, re-weighted, plus noise.A simulated recruiter using a different formula and its own noise.7
No mismatched pairsEvery resume was written for the job it was compared with.30% of resumes are compared with a job outside their own field.7
A backwards explanationA candidate predicted weak was described as “mainly driven by relevant projects”.The sentence now leads with the factors pushing in the predicted direction.11
Parser failures on real-looking filesA wrapped PDF line became a name; wrapped skills were missed; a Master's field was misread; years were lost.Five targeted fixes, each re-tested on sample files and 600 synthetic resumes.12

A demo you can repeat

The folder sample_resumes/ holds three data analyst resumes. Open the app, choose Custom (blank), and enter:

  • Job title: Data Analyst
  • Required skills: sql, python, excel, data visualization, statistics
  • Preferred skills: tableau, power bi, a/b testing
  • Minimum experience: 2 years. Education: Bachelor's.

Untick the bundled pool and tick the sample resumes. You should get:

CandidateScoreVerdictWhy
Arnav (PDF)99.5%Good matchAll five required skills, all three preferred skills, 5 years of experience, projects match.
Rishab (Word)95.1%Good matchFour of five required skills (missing statistics), 2.2 years, one relevant project.
Arsh (PDF)38.3%Poor matchMissing Python, data visualization and statistics. 0.2 years, far below the 2 required.

A candidate's score does not depend on who else is in the pool. Only the rank does.

The limits we found, stated plainly

  • Experience is only a weighted factor. A recent graduate with 0.2 years and four of five required skills scored about 80% for a role needing 3 years. A real recruiter would likely say no. The app has a hard-requirement filter for this.
  • Scores bunch near the top. Many strong candidates show 98 to 99%, so the order among them rests on tiny differences.
  • The labels are simulated. This bears repeating.
  • The similarity feature is weak. TF-IDF compares words, not meaning, and our resumes are written from templates.
  • The parser has limits. No scanned PDFs, weak handling of two-column layouts, a fixed skills list.
  • Fairness is untested. The model never sees names or demographics, but that does not prove it is fair. It is listed as future work in your deck.

If someone asks you

Why Logistic Regression?
It is simple, fast, and every number inside it can be read, so explanations are exact rather than approximate. Slide 5 chose it for that reason.
Why synthetic data?
Real resumes are private and labelled hiring outcomes are rarer still. We made the generation process explicit and tunable, and we say plainly that results reflect the simulation.
How do you know the explanation is right?
For this model SHAP is exact: base value plus contributions equals the model's raw score to about 15 decimal places. That shows it is faithful to the model. It does not show the model is correct.
What would you do next?
Real data, a model that can express hard cut-offs, embeddings instead of TF-IDF, LIME and counterfactual explanations, and a fairness audit. All of these are on your own future-scope slide.

Changing things: five recipes

Teach the parser a new skill nickname

Add one line to ALIASES in skills.py, for example "gke": "kubernetes",. The app uses it at once on restart. The synthetic dataset also draws nicknames from this list, so re-run steps 1 to 4 if you want it included there.

Teach the parser a new skill name

Add it to BUILTIN_SKILLS in resume_parser.py. Remember that any skill you type as a requirement is always searched for anyway.

Make the pretend recruiter pickier

Raise LABEL_THRESHOLD in author_dataset.py (for example to 0.60). Fewer candidates are labelled good. Re-run steps 1 to 4, then compare the metrics.

Add a new job template

In author_dataset.py: add a dictionary to JOBS, add three projects for it to RELEVANT_PROJECTS, and add its fields to JOB_FIELDS. Re-run steps 1 to 4. The app will list it as a template.

Add an eighth feature

  1. Write the calculation inside compute_features in feature_engineering.py.
  2. Add its name to the FEATURES list in train_model.py. Note that explain_shap.py and report_candidate.py keep their own copies of this list, so update those too, plus the FEATURE_LABELS and phrase tables in report_candidate.py.
  3. Re-run steps 2 to 4.
