Chapter 18 · Part IV · Wrap-up

Check yourself

Quiz

Try to answer each question in your head or on paper before opening it. If you can answer most of these, you understand the project.

1. What is a feature, and what are our seven?

A number that measures one useful property of an example. Ours: required-skill match, preferred-skill match, experience match, education match, technology match, project relevance and semantic (text) similarity. Each is computed for a resume against a specific job.

2. What is a label, and where does ours come from?

The correct answer for an example: 1 for good match, 0 for poor. Ours comes from a simulated recruiter in author_dataset.py, a program that scores each candidate's true attributes, adds some noise, and applies a pass mark.

3. Why do we split the data into practice and exam sets?

To measure how the model performs on examples it has never seen. Testing on the practice set would only measure memory and would hide overfitting.

4. What does random.seed(42) do?

It makes the random numbers repeatable. The same seed produces the same sequence, so the dataset and the split are identical on every run.

5. Why does skill normalization matter?

Without it, “k8s” and “Kubernetes” are different strings, and a candidate would be marked as missing a skill they have. Normalization maps every spelling to one official name before comparing.

6. Why does mentions("I know JavaScript", "java") return False?

The pattern requires that the characters before and after java are not letters or digits. In “javascript” the next character is the letter “s”, so there is no whole-word match.

7. What does the sigmoid function do in Logistic Regression?

It squeezes the raw weighted sum, which can be any number, into the range 0 to 1 so it can be read as a probability.

8. A feature has weight 4.48 and a candidate's value is 0.2 above the average. What is that feature's SHAP contribution?

weight × (value − average) = 4.48 × 0.2 = +0.90. Positive, so it pushes toward a good match.

9. The model said “good” for 56 candidates and 49 of them really were good. What is the precision?

Precision = correct “good” answers ÷ all “good” answers = 49 ÷ 56 = 0.875.

10. Why does the simulated recruiter use a different formula from the model's features?

If both used the same formula, the model could simply reproduce it and score nearly perfectly, which would prove nothing. A different formula, with noise, forces the model to learn an approximation.

11. Why does the app need st.session_state?

Streamlit re-runs the whole script on every click. Without saving the ranking in session state, it would vanish the moment you clicked a table row.

12. What is a parser warning, and why show it?

A note saying a field could not be found, for example no Projects section. It is shown so the user knows a low score may come from the parser's gap and not from the candidate.

13. Why does the app reuse the saved tfidf.pkl rather than fitting a new vectorizer?

A new vectorizer would learn a different vocabulary and word weights, putting similarity numbers on a different scale from the one the model trained on. The model would then misread them.

14. Why use cross-validation as well as one test split?

One exam can be lucky or unlucky. Repeating the learn-and-test cycle five times on different slices and averaging gives a steadier estimate, and the spread shows how stable the model is.

15. Name two limitations of this project.

Any two of: the labels are simulated; experience is a weighted factor rather than a hard cut-off; TF-IDF compares words, not meaning; the parser cannot read scanned PDFs; scores bunch near the top; fairness has not been audited; SHAP explains the model, not the truth.

Exercises

Doing teaches more than reading. These are in rising order of difficulty.

  1. Break and fix. Delete the “Projects” heading from a copy of Rishab.docx, upload it, and read the warning. What happened to its score, and why?
  2. Move the pass mark. Change LABEL_THRESHOLD to 0.60, re-run steps 1 to 4, and compare the accuracy, precision and recall. Which went up and which went down?
  3. Find a disagreement. Run python src/report_candidate.py --list, look for a row where the model and the label disagree, and use SHAP to explain in three sentences why the model was wrong.
  4. Upload your own resume. Parse it. Which skills did it miss? Add them to BUILTIN_SKILLS and try again.
  5. Explain it to a friend. In under 100 words, without jargon, say what this project does and why the explanation matters.
  6. Extend it. Add an eighth feature, such as years of experience beyond the minimum, following the recipe in chapter 17. Does accuracy change?

Glossary

Accuracy
The share of all answers that were right.
Alias
A nickname for a skill, such as “k8s” for Kubernetes.
API
A way for one program to use another's service over the internet, with a key as a password.
Black box
A model whose reasoning cannot be inspected.
Class
A blueprint for bundling data and functions together. Ours is Artifacts.
Classification
Sorting examples into groups. Ours has two: good match and poor match.
Comprehension
A loop written as one expression, like [x for x in items if x > 3].
Confusion matrix
A table counting correct answers and each kind of mistake.
Cosine similarity
A 0-to-1 measure of how alike two lists of numbers are, by the angle between them.
Cross-validation
Repeating the practice-and-exam cycle on different slices of data and averaging the marks.
CSV
A table saved as plain text, one row per line.
DataFrame
A table inside Python, from the pandas library.
Dictionary
A collection of key-value pairs, looked up by key.
Docstring
A note in triple quotes describing a file or function.
Feature
A number measuring one useful property of an example.
Function
A named recipe you can run many times.
Intercept
The starting number a model adds before the weighted features.
JSON
A plain-text format for lists and dictionaries.
Label
The correct answer attached to an example.
Latent variable
A hidden number used to generate data, which the model never sees. Ours is q.
Log-odds
The model's raw score before the sigmoid. SHAP values are measured in it.
Logistic Regression
A model that adds up weighted features and squashes the total into a probability.
Normalization
Making equal things look equal, such as mapping every spelling of a skill to one name.
Overfitting
Memorising practice examples instead of learning the pattern.
Parsing
Pulling structured facts out of messy text.
Precision
When the model says “good”, how often it is right.
Recall
Of the truly good cases, how many the model found.
Regex
A language for describing the shape of text, used to find dates, emails and headings.
ROC-AUC
How often the model scores a random good example above a random poor one. 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing.
Seed
A starting number that makes random choices repeatable.
Session state
Streamlit's notebook that survives re-runs of the script.
Set
A collection with no duplicates and no order.
SHAP
A method that splits a prediction into one fair contribution per feature.
Sigmoid
The curve that turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.
Stop words
Very common words (the, and, of) ignored when comparing texts.
Synthetic data
Data made up by a program rather than collected from real life.
TF-IDF
A way to turn text into numbers that makes rare, distinctive words count more than common ones.
Train/test split
Dividing data into examples to learn from and examples to be marked on.
Weight
A number saying how much one feature matters to the model.

Where to go next

  • Python: the official tutorial at docs.python.org (search “Python tutorial”), and the first ten chapters of any beginner book.
  • Tables: the “10 minutes to pandas” page in the pandas documentation.
  • Machine learning: the scikit-learn user guide, especially its sections on model evaluation and cross-validation.
  • Explainability: Interpretable Machine Learning by Christoph Molnar, free to read online, and the SHAP documentation.
  • Regular expressions: regex101.com, which explains each part of a pattern as you type.
  • Web apps in Python: the Streamlit documentation.

You have now met the whole pipeline, from invented resumes to a ranked list with reasons. The best next step is to change something small, run it, and see what happens.
